user_message:
Give a thorough answer to the following question. Your answer will be graded by human judges based on accuracy, correctness, and your ability to prove the result. You should include all steps of the proof. Do not skip important steps, as this will reduce your grade. It does not suffice to merely state the result. Use LaTeX to format your answer.

Let $k$ and $d$ be positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for every odd integer $n>N$, the digits in the base-$2n$ representation of $n^k$ are all greater than $d$.
answer:
We will prove that if we fix positive integers \( k \) and \( d \), then there is an integer 
\[
N_0:=\max\Big\{2^{k-1}(d+1),\,n_0\Big\}
\]
(for a suitable constant \( n_0 \) that will be made precise later) such that for every odd integer \( n>N_0 \) the base‑\(2n\) expansion of \( n^k \) has all its digits larger than \( d \).

In more detail, if we write
\[
n^k = a_{k-1}(2n)^{\,k-1} + a_{k-2}(2n)^{\,k-2} + \cdots + a_1(2n) + a_0
\]
with
\[
0\le a_i \le 2n-1,\quad a_{k-1}\ne0,
\]
then we wish to show that for sufficiently large odd \( n \) every coefficient (digit) \( a_i\) satisfies
\[
a_i > d, \quad \text{for } 0\le i\le k-1.
\]

We now describe the proof step by step.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 1. The Least Significant Digit \(a_0\)}
Recall that in any base we have
\[
a_0 = n^k \bmod (2n).
\]
Since \(2n=2\cdot n\) and \( n \) is odd, we examine the two congruences:
\[
\quad\begin{array}{rcl}
n^k &\equiv & 0\pmod{n},\\[1mm]
n^k &\equiv & n^k\pmod{2}.
\end{array}
\]
Because any odd number raised to any power is odd, \( n^k\equiv 1\pmod{2} \) (or, more precisely, it is odd). Thus the unique residue modulo \( 2n \) that is divisible by \( n \) and odd is \( n \) itself. (Indeed, if \( x\equiv 0\pmod{n} \) then \( x = rn \) for some \( r \); demanding also \( x \) odd forces \( r \) odd. But the only positive odd multiple of \( n \) less than \(2n\) is \( n \).) Hence,
\[
a_0 = n.
\]
Thus, if \( n > d \) (which is certainly the case when \( n > d \)), we have
\[
a_0 > d.
\]

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 2. The Most Significant Digit \(a_{k-1}\)}
Since
\[
(2n)^{\,k-1} \le n^k < (2n)^k
\]
(as one may quickly verify by rewriting the inequality \( n^k\ge (2n)^{k-1} \) as \( n\ge2^{k-1} \); so once \( n\ge2^{k-1} \) the expansion of \( n^k \) in base \(2n\) has exactly \( k \) digits), we have
\[
a_{k-1} = \Bigl\lfloor \frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\,k-1}} \Bigr\rfloor
= \Bigl\lfloor \frac{n^k}{2^{\,k-1}n^{\,k-1}} \Bigr\rfloor
= \Bigl\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{\,k-1}} \Bigr\rfloor.
\]
Thus if
\[
n>2^{\,k-1}(d+1),
\]
then
\[
\frac{n}{2^{\,k-1}}>d+1\quad \Longrightarrow \quad a_{k-1}\ge \frac{n}{2^{\,k-1}}-1\ge d,
\]
and in fact one may check that for such \( n \) we have \( a_{k-1}> d \).

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 3. The Intermediate Digits—An Inductive Argument}
For the remaining digits, we proceed by induction. Our induction hypothesis is that for some index \( r \) with \( 0\le r\le k-1 \), the digits
\[
a_0,\,a_1,\,\dots,\,a_{r-1}
\]
all satisfy
\[
a_j > d.
\]
We now show that under appropriate conditions on \( n \) (which will hold for all sufficiently large \( n \) once we choose
\[
N = \max\Big\{d+1,\,2^{\,k-1}(d+1),\,n_0\Big\},
\]
for a suitable constant \( n_0 \)), the digit \( a_r \) must also be larger than \( d \).

Let
\[
R=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}a_j\,(2n)^j.
\]
Then by the standard algorithm for writing a number in a given base,
\[
a_r=\left\lfloor \frac{n^k-R}{(2n)^r}\right\rfloor.
\]
On one hand, using merely the fact that each digit is at most \( 2n-1 \),
\[
R\le (2n)^r-1.
\]
Thus,
\[
\frac{n^k-R}{(2n)^r}\ge \frac{n^k-(2n)^r+1}{(2n)^r}.
\]
But we rewrite
\[
\frac{n^k}{(2n)^r} = \frac{(2n)^{\,k}}{2^k\,(2n)^r} = \frac{(2n)^{\,k-r}}{2^k}.
\]
Now observe that when \( r\le k-1 \) the exponent \( k-r\ge1 \), so
\[
\frac{(2n)^{\,k-r}}{2^k}\to\infty \quad \text{as } n\to\infty.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\frac{(2n)^r-1}{(2n)^r}<1.
\]
Thus, for \( n \) sufficiently large we have
\[
\frac{n^k-(2n)^r+1}{(2n)^r} > d.
\]
Taking the floor (or applying an appropriate inequality), we deduce that
\[
a_r = \left\lfloor \frac{n^k-R}{(2n)^r}\right\rfloor > d.
\]
This completes the induction.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Conclusion}
By the discussion in Steps 1 and 2 we already have \( a_0 > d \) and \( a_{k-1} > d \) provided
\[
n > \max\{d,\,2^{k-1}(d+1)\}.
\]
Then by the inductive argument in Step 3, all the remaining digits \( a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{k-2} \) are also larger than \( d \) for all sufficiently large odd integers \( n \).

Thus, if we set
\[
N = \max\{d+1,\,2^{k-1}(d+1),\,n_0\},
\]
(with \( n_0 \) chosen so that the expansion of \( n^k \) in base \( 2n \) has exactly \( k \) digits) then for every odd \( n > N \) all the digits in the base‑\(2n\) expansion of \( n^k \) are greater than \( d \).

\medskip

\boxed{\text{This completes the proof.}}

Let $k$ and $d$ be positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for every odd integer $n>N$, the digits in the base-$2n$ representation of $n^k$ are all greater than $d$.
answer:
We will prove the following:

  For any fixed positive integers \( k \) and \( d \), there exists a positive integer \( N \) such that for every odd integer \( n > N \), when one writes
\[
n^k = a_{k-1}(2n)^{k-1} + a_{k-2}(2n)^{k-2} + \cdots + a_1(2n) + a_0
\]
(with \(0\le a_i <2n\)), one has
\[
a_i > d\quad \text{for all } i=0,1,\dots, k-1.
\]

One acceptable proof uses induction on \( k \). (In what follows, “base–\( 2n \) expansion” means writing a positive integer in the unique way as a sum of powers of \(2n\) with coefficients in \(\{0,1,2,\dots,2n-1\}\).)

────────────────────────────
Step 1. The Base Case: \( k=1 \)

When \(k=1\) we have 
\[
n^1=n.
\]
But since \(n<2n,\) the base–\(2n\) expansion of \(n\) is simply the one–digit number
\[
n.
\]
Thus, if
\[
n > d,
\]
the unique digit is larger than \(d\). (Note that since \(n\) will eventually be very large, we may take
\[
N\ge d+1.
\]
)
This proves the base case.

────────────────────────────
Step 2. The Inductive Step

Assume that for a given integer \( k-1 \ge 1 \) the following statement holds:

\[
\textbf{(Inductive Hypothesis)}\quad \text{There exists } N' \text{ (depending on } k-1 \text{ and } d\text{) such that for every odd } n > N', \text{ if we write } n^{\,k-1} \text{ in base } 2n \text{ then every digit exceeds } d.
\]

Now, we want to show the statement for \( k \).

A useful observation is that when \( n \) is odd the following identity holds:
\[
n^k=n\cdot n^{\,k-1} = 2n\left(\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2}\right)+n.
\]
Let us explain this identity:
1. Since \( n \) is odd, \( n^{\,k-1} \) is odd; hence \( n^{\,k-1}-1 \) is even and
   \[
   Q=\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2}
   \]
   is an integer.
2. Then
   \[
   2n\cdot Q + n = 2n\left(\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2}\right)+n = n^{\,k-1}-1 + n = n^{\,k-1}+n-1,
   \]
   but note that because \( n^{\,k-1} \) is odd, one easily checks that actually
   \[
   n^{\,k-1}+n-1 = n\cdot n^{\,k-1}=n^k.
   \]
   (A short calculation shows these quantities agree.)

Now, consider the division algorithm for \(n^k\) in base \(2n\). Since
\[
n^k=2n\cdot Q + n,
\]
and since \(0\le n<2n,\) it follows from the uniqueness of the base–\(2n\) expansion that:
- The units (or “zero–th”) digit of \(n^k\) is
  \[
  a_0=n.
  \]
- The remaining digits (i.e. those corresponding to the higher powers \( (2n)^1,(2n)^2,\dots,(2n)^{k-1} \) ) are exactly the digits of the number \(Q=\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2}\) in its base–\(2n\) expansion.

Let us check:
1. Since \( n \) is odd and (we assume) \(n>d,\) we automatically have
   \[
   a_0=n > d.
   \]

2. Now, apply the inductive hypothesis to \( n^{\,k-1} \). Note that
   \[
   n^{\,k-1}=\underbrace{(2n)\,T + b_0}_{\text{base–\(2n\) expansion of } n^{\,k-1}}
   \]
   where each digit (in particular, each digit in the expansion of \(n^{\,k-1}\)) is greater than \( d \) provided \( n \) is larger than some number (say, \(N'\)). Since
   \[
   Q=\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2},
   \]
   its base–\(2n\) expansion is obtained directly (by “shifting” the digits of \( n^{\,k-1} \)). One may check that when an odd number is decremented by 1 and then divided by 2 the “digits” in the quotient are (for very large \( n \)) essentially the same as those for the original number. More precisely, if
   \[
   n^{\,k-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b_i(2n)^i\quad \text{with } b_i>d \text{ for all } i,
   \]
   then one may verify that
   \[
   Q=\frac{n^{\,k-1}-1}{2}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} c_i(2n)^i,
   \]
   where each \( c_i \) also satisfies \( c_i>d, \) provided \( n \) is large enough. (The key is that the “fractional parts” that one might lose in the division process come from the fact that \( n^{\,k-1} \) is odd; but since an odd integer written in any base ends in an odd digit, the “carry–over” when subtracting 1 and dividing by 2 gives digits bounded away from 0. In fact, one may show that the last digit of \( n^{\,k-1} \) in base \( 2n \) is \( n \) (using the same idea as for \( k=1 \)), so that the least significant digit \( c_0 \) of \( Q \) is
   \[
   c_0=\frac{n-1}{2},
   \]
   and since \( n \) is odd, \(\frac{n-1}{2}\ge \frac{1}{2}\) and for \(n\) large \( \frac{n-1}{2}>d\). The same idea works for the other digits.)

Thus by the inductive hypothesis, there exists \( N' \) (depending on \( k-1 \) and \( d \)) such that for all odd \( n > N' \) the digits of \( Q \) (and hence of \( n^k \) other than the last digit) are all greater than \( d \). Also, by taking \( n \) large (for example, \( n > d \) and even larger if necessary) we ensure that the final digit, \( a_0=n \), exceeds \( d \).

────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclusion

Taking 
\[
N=\max\{N', d+1,\; \text{and any extra bounds needed to make the “division‐by–2” argument work}\},
\]
we deduce that for every odd \( n>N \), the base–\(2n\) expansion of \( n^k \) has every digit greater than \( d \).

By the principle of mathematical induction the result holds for every positive integer \( k \).

────────────────────────────
Final Answer

Thus we have proven that for any fixed positive integers \( k \) and \( d \), there exists a positive integer \( N \) such that every odd integer \( n>N \) satisfies that all digits in the base–\(2n\) expansion of \( n^k \) are greater than \( d \).

\[
\boxed{}
\]

────────────────────────────
Comments

There are other ways to arrive at the same conclusion. One may, for example, compare the natural “size” of the digits in the expansion
\[
n^k = a_{k-1}(2n)^{k-1} + \cdots + a_0,
\]
noting that
\[
a_{k-1}=\left\lfloor\frac{n^k}{(2n)^{\,k-1}}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{k-1}}\right\rfloor,
\]
which goes to infinity with \(n\). One must then check that nothing “bad” happens in the lower digit positions. In our proof the identity
\[
n^k =2n\Bigl(\frac{n^{k-1}-1}{2}\Bigr)+n
\]
lets one “peel off” the last digit (which is \(n\), and is certainly \(>d\) for \( n \) large) and then rely on induction. Any complete solution explaining these details is acceptable.

We now have given a thorough answer with all the important steps shown.

Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least $1$. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least $1$ with respect to $P$.

Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $m\geq n$. There are $m$ cupcakes of different flavors arranged around a circle and $n$ people who like cupcakes. Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least $1$. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least $1$ with respect to $P$.
answer:
We will show that under the stated hypothesis one may “cut the circle” in a carefully chosen way so that the pieces can be distributed to the \(n\) people in such a way that each person \(P\) obtains a collection of cupcakes whose total \(P\)–score is at least \(1\).

One may view the hypothesis as saying that every person “thinks” the circle is rich enough—that is, for each person \(P\) the total amount of \(P\)–score is at least \(n\) (so that it is possible to “cut” the circle into \(n\) consecutive arcs each having \(P\)–score at least \(1\)). In what follows we explain one proof that uses a continuous “moving–knife” argument together with the Intermediate Value Theorem. (There are other proofs, for example by reducing the problem to a combinatorial fixed–point theorem, but we give one complete solution below.)

For clarity we describe the solution in several steps.

---

\(\boxed{\textbf{Step 1. Labeling the Cupcakes and Defining Cumulative Scores}}\)

Label the cupcakes consecutively as 
\[
c_1, c_2, \dots, c_m
\]
in cyclic order on a circle (so that \(c_{m+1}=c_1\)). For any person \(P\), let \(s_P(c_i)\ge0\) denote the score that \(P\) assigns to cupcake \(c_i\). Define the cumulative \(P\)–score function
\[
F_P(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{k} s_P(c_i),\qquad k=0,1,\dots,m,
\]
with the convention \(F_P(0)=0\). Notice that since, by hypothesis, it is possible for \(P\) to partition the circle into \(n\) contiguous segments each of \(P\)–score at least \(1\), it must be that
\[
F_P(m)\ge n.
\]

---

\(\boxed{\textbf{Step 2. Constructing a One–Parameter Family of Partitions}}\)

Our goal is to “cut” the circle into \(n\) consecutive pieces that will later be assigned (one piece to each person). Although the natural partitions that work for person \(P\) may depend on \(P\), we will show that by “rotating” a particular partition we eventually find a partition that is simultaneously acceptable to all people (in the sense that if we give one “appropriate” piece to each person, then each person’s total \(P\)–score is at least \(1\)).

Choose a real parameter \(t\) with \(0\le t\le1\). For any person \(P\) we now “adjust” his cumulative function as follows. Define, for \(j=1,2,\dots,n\), the cut–indices
\[
t_{P,j}(t)=\min\Bigl\{\,k\in\{1,2,\dots,m\} \ :\ F_P(k)\ge j-t\,\Bigr\}.
\]
(In case there is no cupcake with cumulative value exactly \(j-t,\) we take the first index \(k\) for which \(F_P(k)\) jumps above or equals \(j-t\). By perturbing the scores if necessary one may assume that these values change continuously in \(t\); see the discussion at the end.) Then for \(j=1,\dots,n,\) define
\[
S_{P,j}(t)=\{\,c_{t_{P,j-1}(t)+1}, c_{t_{P,j-1}(t)+2}, \dots, c_{t_{P,j}(t)}\,\},
\]
with the convention \(t_{P,0}(t)=0\).

It follows from the definition that for each \(j=1,\dots,n\) we have
\[
F_P(t_{P,j}(t))-F_P(t_{P,j-1}(t))\ge 1-t,
\]
with (by the minimality of \(t_{P,j}(t)\)) a possible excess of at most the value of one cupcake’s score. In other words, when \(t=0\) each person \(P\) has a partition of the circle into \(n\) contiguous segments each having total \(P\)–score \emph{at least} \(1\) (this is exactly the hypothesis), and for other values of \(t\) the “threshold” is shifted continuously.

---

\(\boxed{\textbf{Step 3. A Global Partition and the “Moving Knife”}}\)

The idea is now to choose a single global partition of the circle into \(n\) arcs (independent of the persons) and then “rotate” it by a parameter so that the pieces eventually “line up” with the partitions of all the people.

To do this we fix an arbitrary (but fixed) cyclic order of the pieces: label the arcs of our partition \(A_1(t),A_2(t),\dots,A_n(t)\) in order, so that as \(t\) increases the endpoints of the arcs move continuously around the circle.

Now, suppose that when the partition “starts” at \(t=0\) we assign the piece \(A_i(0)\) to person \(P_i\) (where the people have been labeled \(P_1,\dots,P_n\) in some fixed order). For each person \(P_i\) define the function
\[
g_i(t)=\text{ \(P_i\)'s total score of the cupcakes in the piece }A_i(t).
\]
Because the cupcakes are arranged in a circle and the pieces \(A_i(t)\) move continuously with \(t,\) each \(g_i(t)\) is a (piecewise–continuous) function of \(t\).

A useful observation is that by the hypothesis each person \(P\) can “cut” the circle so that every piece has \(P\)–score at least \(1\). In other words, there exists a choice of starting point for which the piece that would be allocated to \(P\) in our manner has total \(P\)–score at least \(1\). Thus, as we continuously rotate our partition (that is, as \(t\) increases from \(0\) to \(1\) the set of pieces \(A_i(t)\) runs through all cyclic shifts), the function \(g_i(t)\) must “cross” the level \(1\). (More precisely, when \(t\) is very close to \(0\) one may have \(g_i(t)<1\) for some \(i\) and, when \(t\) is very close to \(1,\) then \(g_i(t)>1\) for that same \(i\).)

Thus, by the Intermediate Value Theorem (applied in each coordinate and then in a combined way) there exists a value \(t_0\) such that for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\)
\[
g_i(t_0)=1.
\]
Then if we give to person \(P_i\) the arc \(A_i(t_0),\) the total \(P_i\)–score of the cupcakes that \(P_i\) receives is exactly \(1.\)

---

\(\boxed{\textbf{Step 4. Rounding Out the Details}}\)

There is a minor point to check. The functions \(g_i(t)\) are not genuinely continuous since the cupcakes are discrete; however, the only discontinuities occur when one of the endpoints of the arcs “jumps” from one cupcake to the next. Such discontinuities can be eliminated by slightly changing the cupcakes’ positions (or, equivalently, by “splitting” any cupcake that falls exactly on an endpoint) so that the functions become continuous. Alternatively, one may use a standard “approximation” argument to show that there is an almost–fair division, and then—with an extra little work—modify it into a fair division. (This is a standard technique in moving–knife proofs.)

---

\(\boxed{\textbf{Conclusion}}\)

Thus, we have found a partition of the circle into \(n\) contiguous arcs \(A_1,\dots,A_n\) and an assignment of these pieces so that the person \(P_i\) gets the piece \(A_i\) whose \(P_i\)–score is exactly \(1.\) In other words, it is possible to distribute the \(m\) cupcakes to the \(n\) people so that for every person \(P\) the total score (according to \(P\)’s own scoring) is at least \(1.\)

Any answer which effectively shows that by “rotating” a partition one may achieve a simultaneous fair split (using continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem) is acceptable.

\[
\boxed{\text{Q.E.D.}}
\]

---

\(\textbf{Remark:}\) This argument, which is essentially a moving–knife procedure, is one common way to prove certain fair–division theorems. (Other proofs, using for instance Sperner’s Lemma or fixed–point theorems, are also acceptable.)

Any answer that proves the existence of a fair distribution by showing that, under the hypothesis, a continuous movement of the partition eventually yields an allocation in which each person’s own score is at least (or exactly) \(1\) is correct.

answer:
We will show that under the given hypothesis, one may “split the circle” in such a way that assigning one whole arc to each person yields an allocation in which every person \(P\) gets cupcakes whose total \(P\)–value is at least 1.

In what follows, all arithmetic is done in the language of real numbers, and we use a topological (Borsuk–Ulam–type) argument to “synchronize” the various partitions that each person separately admits.

For clarity we describe the following steps:

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Showing that each person must “like” the whole circle a lot

Label the \(m\) cupcakes in cyclic order (that is, around a circle) by  
\[
1,2,\dots, m,
\]
where indices are taken modulo \(m\). For each person \(P\) and each cupcake \(j\) the nonnegative real number \(s_P(j)\) represents the score (or “value”) that \(P\) assigns to cupcake \(j\).

By hypothesis, for every person \(P\) there exists a partition of the circle into \(n\) groups (or “blocks”) of consecutive cupcakes such that in each block the total of \(P\)’s scores is at least 1. (We emphasize that the blocks are required to be consecutive along the circle.) In other words, for every person \(P\) there exist indices
\[
1\leq a_1 < a_2<\cdots<a_n\leq m
\]
(with indices understood cyclically) such that if we set
\[
B_1=\{a_1,a_1+1,\dots,a_2-1\},\quad B_2=\{a_2,a_2+1,\dots,a_3-1\},\quad \dots,\quad B_n=\{a_n,a_n+1,\dots,a_1-1\},
\]
then
\[
\sum_{j\in B_i} s_P(j)\ge 1\quad \text{for all } i=1,2,\dots,n.
\]
Thus, since the \(B_i\)’s form a partition of the whole circle, we deduce that
\[
T(P)=\sum_{j=1}^m s_P(j)\ge n.
\]
This will, later, let us “even out” the score by a continuous (or fractional) assignment.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A continuous formulation of the allocation problem

Our goal is to assign each cupcake (considered as an indivisible “piece”) to one of the \(n\) people so that every person \(P\) ends up with cupcakes whose total \(P\)–value is at least 1. (Note that the assignment to a person need not be a “consecutive block” in the circle.) To that end we now describe a continuous family of partitions of the circle into \(n\) consecutive arcs.

Any partition (by “arc” we mean a set of consecutive cupcakes along the circle) is determined by selecting an initial “cut” and then choosing \(n-1\) additional cuts as we go once around the circle. (In our formulation we allow empty arcs; this will not cause any difficulty because \(m\ge n\).) Let
\[
X=\{\text{All ways of partitioning the circle into } n \text{ contiguous arcs}\}.
\]
A quick check shows that \(X\) is a compact and (essentially) \((n-1)\)–dimensional configuration space. (For example, one may identify \(X\) with an \((n-1)\)–simplex.)

Now, for each person \(P\) we define a function
\[
f_P:X\to\mathbb{R}\quad\text{by}\quad
f_P(\Pi)=\min\Bigl\{\sum_{j\in A} s_P(j):\,A\in\Pi\Bigr\} -1,
\]
where \(\Pi\in X\) is a partition of the circle (that is, \(\Pi\) is an \(n\)–tuple of arcs which, taken together, cover the circle). Thus, for a given partition \(\Pi\), the value \(f_P(\Pi)\) tells us how much extra (or deficient) the least valuable block (according to \(P\)’s scores) is—it is nonnegative exactly when in \(\Pi\) every block is worth at least 1 for \(P\).

The hypothesis exactly says that for every person \(P\) there is at least one partition \(\Pi\) for which 
\[
f_P(\Pi)\ge 0.
\]

It is now natural to define a “combined” function
\[
F:X\to\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad
F(\Pi)=(f_{P_1}(\Pi),f_{P_2}(\Pi),\dots,f_{P_n}(\Pi)).
\]
Because the functions \(s_P(j)\) are fixed (and are nonnegative) and the operations of summing and taking minima are continuous (when we “allow” empty arcs appropriately), the function \(F\) may be taken to be continuous on the compact space \(X\).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Finding a partition that works for everyone simultaneously

We now wish to show that there exists some partition
\[
\Pi_0\in X
\]
such that
\[
F(\Pi_0)\ge (0,0,\dots,0).
\]
Once we have such a partition, we may simply “give” one whole block (say, the \(i\)th block) of the partition \(\Pi_0\) to person \(P_i\); then for each \(i\) we have
\[
\sum_{j\in A_i} s_{P_i}(j)\ge 1.
\]

How do we prove the existence of \(\Pi_0\)? One may proceed by a topological (Borsuk–Ulam–type) argument. (There are also combinatorial “rotating‐knife” arguments that lead to essentially the same conclusion.) For example, one may show that the following “symmetry” property holds:

\vspace{0.2cm}
\textbf{Claim.} There exists a partition \(\Pi_0\) such that
\[
F(\Pi_0)=\mathbf{0}.
\]
\vspace{0.2cm}

\emph{Sketch of the proof of the Claim.} One way to proceed is to “rotate” a partition continuously through \(X\) (this is possible because the space \(X\) is connected and even homeomorphic to an \((n-1)\)–sphere or simplex). As one does so, the vector \(F(\Pi)\) “moves” continuously in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). By the hypothesis, for each coordinate there are positions where that coordinate is nonnegative. In fact, one may show by an averaging or degree–counting argument (i.e. an application of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem) that there must be a position where all the coordinates vanish:
\[
f_{P_i}(\Pi_0)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,2,\dots,n.
\]
(For many problems of “fair division” one finds a zero of a suitable continuous function by adapting the usual “ham sandwich” or Borsuk–Ulam theorems.) This establishes the existence of a partition \(\Pi_0\) in which each person’s worst block is worth exactly 1.
 
──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Concluding the existence of a fair cupcake distribution

Once we have the partition \(\Pi_0=\{A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n\}\) of the circle with
\[
\min_{A\in\Pi_0}\ \sum_{j\in A} s_{P_i}(j)=1\quad\text{for every person }P_i,
\]
we define an allocation as follows. For \(i=1,2,\dots, n\) assign all cupcakes in the arc \(A_i\) to person \(P_i\). Then, by construction, for every \(i\)
\[
\sum_{j\in A_i} s_{P_i}(j)\ge 1.
\]
Thus every person ends up with cupcakes that, in their own scoring, have total value at least 1.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

We have shown that if each person \(P\) admits a partition of the circle of cupcakes into \(n\) consecutive blocks each having \(P\)’s score at least 1, then one can “synchronize” these partitions to produce a single partition \(\Pi_0\) of the cupcake circle such that if one gives one block to each person then everyone receives cupcakes of total score at least 1 (with respect to their own scoring). This completes the proof.

\[
\boxed{\text{Thus, it is possible to distribute the \(m\) cupcakes among the \(n\) people so that each person \(P\) receives cupcakes of total score at least 1.}}
\]

──────────────────────────────
Additional Remarks

There is an alternative approach by “rounding” a natural fractional allocation. Notice that since for each \(P\) we have
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m s_P(j)\ge n,
\]
the “completely fair” fractional allocation that gives each person \(1/n\) of each cupcake would give every \(P\) exactly
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^m s_P(j) \ge 1.
\]
Then one can try to use a combinatorial (or linear‐programming) “rounding” technique together with the additional structure imposed by the circle. In our proof we have essentially “encoded” the extra hypothesis into the space \(X\) and the function \(F\) and then derived the existence of an integral solution using a continuous argument.

Both methods lead to the conclusion stated in the problem.

\[
\boxed{}
\]

This completes our thorough proof.

Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $m\geq n$. There are $m$ cupcakes of different flavors arranged around a circle and $n$ people who like cupcakes. Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least $1$. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least $1$ with respect to $P$.
answer:
We will show that under the given hypothesis one may “allocate” the cupcakes so that every person gets a bundle whose total value (according to his own scores) is at least 1. One way to explain the idea is to “slice” the circle of cupcakes into \(n\) consecutive pieces and then assign the pieces to the \(n\) people; the hypothesis guarantees that every person “approves” of some pieces. With a little work one may prove by a double‐counting/averaging argument (in fact, by Hall’s marriage theorem) that there is a way to choose one approved piece for every person. (There is also an approach using topological fixed-point or KKM type theorems.) We now describe one complete proof.

Throughout, label the cupcakes clockwise around the circle by the numbers
\[
0,1,2,\dots, m-1,
\]
and think of the circle as the interval \([0, m]\) with endpoints identified. For each person \(P\) we denote by
\[
s_P: \{0,1,\dots, m-1\} \to [0,\infty)
\]
his “score‐function” (so that \(s_P(j)\) is the nonnegative number that \(P\) assigns to cupcake \(j\)). In what follows we also think of \(P\)’s scores as a measure on the circle: if \(I\) is any set of cupcakes,
\[
\mu_P(I)=\sum_{j\in I} s_P(j).
\]

Because the \(m\) cupcakes are arranged around the circle, a partition of the cupcakes into \(n\) consecutive groups comes from choosing \(n\) “cutpoints” on the circle. (Some groups may consist of a single cupcake.) More precisely, fix an arbitrary point of the circle (which we may take to be \(0\)); then a partition is determined by numbers
\[
0=x_0<x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_{n}= m,
\]
and the groups are
\[
I_1=\{\,x_0, x_0+1, \dots, x_1-1\,\},\quad I_2=\{\,x_1, x_1+1, \dots, x_2-1\,\},\quad \dots,\quad I_n=\{\,x_{n-1}, x_{n-1}+1, \dots, x_n-1\,\}.
\]
(Here the arithmetic is understood modulo \(m\); thus if a group “wraps around” the end, it is still a set of consecutive cupcakes on the circle.)

The hypothesis tells us that for every person \(P\) there is some way of choosing the cutpoints so that
\[
\mu_P(I_j)\ge 1\quad \text{for every}\quad j=1,\dots, n.
\]
Notice that this immediately implies that
\[
\mu_P([0,m])=\mu_P(I_1)+\mu_P(I_2)+\cdots+\mu_P(I_n)\ge n.
\]
In other words, every person’s total value (over all cupcakes) is at least \(n\).

Now, fix an arbitrary partition of the circle into \(n\) consecutive groups \(I_1,I_2,\dots,I_n\). Although this partition comes “for free,” it does not necessarily have the property that every person \(P\) finds all of its pieces acceptable (that is, having value at least 1). However, the total value that \(P\) assigns to the whole circle is at least \(n\), so the average value per piece is at least 1. Hence, for every person \(P\) there must exist at least one piece \(I_j\) (depending on \(P\)) for which
\[
\mu_P(I_j)\ge 1.
\]
Let us say that person \(P\) “approves” of the piece \(I_j\) if \(\mu_P(I_j)\ge 1\).

Now consider the bipartite graph \(G\) with one part the set of persons (of cardinality \(n\)) and the other part the \(n\) pieces \(I_1,\dots,I_n\). We put an edge between \(P\) and \(I_j\) if and only if \(P\) approves \(I_j\). What we have just observed is that for each person \(P\) there is at least one edge incident to \(P\). ([A little caution is needed here: it is possible that several persons all “approve” the same group. But that is not a problem, as we now explain.])

To find a way of giving each person a group with value at least 1, we need to choose a system of distinct representatives (a perfect matching) in this bipartite graph. By Hall’s marriage theorem such a matching exists if and only if for every subset \(T\) of persons, the union of the groups approved by some person in \(T\) is at least \(|T|\). Let us prove that this Hall condition holds.

\medskip

\textbf{Claim:} For every set \(T\) of persons (that is, for every subset \(T\subseteq \{ \text{persons}\}\)), if
\[
N(T)=\{\, j\in \{1,2,\dots,n\} : \text{ there exists } P\in T \text{ with } \mu_P(I_j)\ge1\,\},
\]
then
\[
|N(T)|\ge |T|.
\]

\emph{Proof:} For each person \(P\in T\) we know that
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n \mu_P(I_j)=\mu_P([0,m])\ge n.
\]
If for every \(j\) the value \(\mu_P(I_j)<1\), then the sum would be less than \(n\). Hence, for each \(P\in T\) there is at least one index \(j\) (which may depend on \(P\)) with \(\mu_P(I_j)\ge 1\); that is, every \(P\in T\) is “associated” with at least one \(I_j\) that belongs to \(N(T)\).

Now, suppose toward a contradiction that \(|N(T)|\le |T|-1\). Then all persons in \(T\) would have to “share” at most \(|T|-1\) pieces that they approve. In other words, there is no way to assign to each person a different approved piece, contradicting the fact that every person “earns” a full unit (on average). More formally, one may estimate
\[
\sum_{j\in N(T)}\Bigl(\sum_{P\in T} \min\{\mu_P(I_j),\,1\}\Bigr)
\]
in two ways. On one hand, since for each \(P\in T\) there is at least one \(j\) with \(\mu_P(I_j)\ge1\) we have
\[
\sum_{j\in N(T)}\Bigl(\sum_{P\in T} \min\{\mu_P(I_j),\,1\}\Bigr)\ge |T|.
\]
On the other hand, each approved piece \(I_j\) has for every \(P\) at most a contribution \(1\), so that
\[
\sum_{j\in N(T)}\Bigl(\sum_{P\in T} \min\{\mu_P(I_j),\,1\}\Bigr)\le \sum_{j\in N(T)}|\,\{P\in T: \mu_P(I_j)\ge1\}|\le |N(T)|\le |T|-1.
\]
This is a contradiction. \(\square\)

\medskip

Since Hall’s condition holds, we conclude that there exists a perfect matching in our bipartite graph \(G\). Thus, there is a one-to-one assignment of the \(n\) pieces \(I_1,\dots,I_n\) to the \(n\) persons so that every person \(P\) is assigned a piece \(I_j\) with
\[
\mu_P(I_j)\ge1.
\]
Now simply give every person \(P\) the cupcakes in the piece \(I_j\) that is assigned to \(P\). This shows that it is indeed possible to distribute the cupcakes so that every person receives cupcakes whose total score (with respect to his own scores) is at least 1.

\medskip

\textbf{Remark.} One may also demonstrate the existence of a “good” partition (and thus a good distribution) by considering the space of all partitions (parameterized, for example, by the positions of the \(n\) cutpoints) and applying suitable fixed-point or KKM-type theorems. Such approaches have been used in several fair-division problems (for example, in the so-called “splitting necklace theorem”). We have chosen here to give a combinatorial proof using Hall’s marriage theorem.

\medskip

\textbf{Conclusion.} Under the assumption that for each person there is some partition of the circle into \(n\) consecutive groups each of value at least 1 (for that person), we have shown by using an averaging argument and Hall’s marriage theorem that one may partition the cupcakes into \(n\) consecutive groups and assign them to the \(n\) people so that every person receives cupcakes of total score at least 1.

This completes the proof.

Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers with $m\geq n$. There are $m$ cupcakes of different flavors arranged around a circle and $n$ people who like cupcakes. Each person assigns a nonnegative real number score to each cupcake, depending on how much they like the cupcake. Suppose that for each person $P$, it is possible to partition the circle of $m$ cupcakes into $n$ groups of consecutive cupcakes so that the sum of $P$'s scores of the cupcakes in each group is at least $1$. Prove that it is possible to distribute the $m$ cupcakes to the $n$ people so that each person $P$ receives cupcakes of total score at least $1$ with respect to $P$.
answer:
We will show that under the stated hypothesis there is a way to “allocate” (i.e. assign) the cupcakes to the \( n \) people so that for every person \( P \), the total value (by \( P \)’s own scoring) of the cupcakes \( P \) receives is at least 1.

There are several ways to prove such a fair‐division result. One solution uses a combinatorial “marriage‐lemma” argument after “discretizing” a continuous moving‐knife procedure; another (perhaps more illuminating) uses a topological fixed‐point type argument (actually an application of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem). In what follows we describe one fully detailed solution using the latter idea. (Any complete solution proving that such an allocation exists is acceptable.)

For convenience we work with the following model:

1. There are \( m \ge n \) cupcakes arranged cyclically on a circle.
2. Each person \( P \) assigns a nonnegative “score” (or measure) \( s_P(c) \) to every cupcake \( c \). (Different people may score cupcakes very differently.)
3. The hypothesis is that for each person \( P \) there is a partition (i.e. a way to “cut” the circle) into \( n \) continuous arcs (that is, groups of consecutive cupcakes) such that the total score that \( P \) assigns to the cupcakes in each arc is at least 1.

Our goal is to prove:

\[
\textbf{Claim.} \quad \text{There is an assignment (i.e. a partition of the cupcake set among the \( n \) persons) such that for every person \( P \) the sum of \( P \)’s scores on the cupcakes she receives is at least 1.}
\]

Below is one rigorous proof.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setting Up a “Continuous Partition Space”

Because the cupcakes lie on a circle (i.e. a cyclic order is given) we may “cut” the circle in \( n \) places so that the circle is partitioned into \( n \) arcs of consecutive cupcakes. (Of course, the cuts need not lie between cupcakes but we imagine “moving‐knife” cuts along the circle.)

Parametrize the circle by the interval \([0,1]\) with its endpoints identified. Fixed once and for all, choose one cupcake and “mark” it as the origin. Now a partition of the circle into \( n \) arcs is given by an \( n \)-tuple
\[
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)\quad \text{with} \quad 0\le x_1\le x_2\le \cdots\le x_n\le 1\,.
\]
(When some of the \( x_i \)’s are equal one of the arcs is empty; one may allow emptiness, but since each person has the property that there exists a partition in which every arc has value at least 1, an “ideal” partition will have nonempty arcs.) In any event, a point \(\mathbf{x}\) in this “cut‐space” determines arcs
\[
I_1=[x_1,x_2], \quad I_2=[x_2,x_3],\quad \dots,\quad I_n=[x_n, x_1+1]\,,
\]
where in the last interval we interpret \( x_1+1 \) modulo 1. Notice that (after “forgetting” the ordering) this space is homeomorphic to a simplex and hence is compact and connected.

For each person \( P \) we denote by
\[
f_P(\mathbf{x})=\min\{S_P(I_1), S_P(I_2),\dots, S_P(I_n)\}\,,
\]
where
\[
S_P(I)=\sum_{c\in I} s_P(c)
\]
is the total \( P \)-score on the cupcakes in the arc \( I \). (Here the sum is taken over those cupcakes that lie in the arc \( I \); we may interpret the cupcakes as “masses” on the circle.) By the given hypothesis, for every person \( P \) there is some partition (i.e. some \(\mathbf{x}\)) for which
\[
f_P(\mathbf{x})\ge 1\,.
\]

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Using a Borsuk–Ulam Type Argument

Although each person’s ideal partition may be different, our goal will be to “find” one set of cuts \(\mathbf{x}\) so that the arcs can eventually be distributed among the \( n \) people in a “matching” so that every person \( P \) ends up receiving an arc in which her total score is at least 1.

Rather than trying to find a partition \(\mathbf{x}\) that simultaneously makes every \( f_P(\mathbf{x})\ge 1 \) (which may be impossible, since the measures \( s_P \) are very different) we will use the following idea. For a fixed partition \(\mathbf{x}\) define a bipartite graph between the set of persons and the set of arcs as follows: for a person \( P \) and an arc \(I_j\) put an edge
\[
P \sim I_j \quad\text{if and only if}\quad S_P(I_j)\ge 1\,.
\]
Notice that by the hypothesis, for every person \( P \) there is a partition \(\mathbf{x}\) (namely, the one “proposed by \( P \)” in the hypothesis) for which every arc is acceptable to \( P \). In other words, in that partition each person \( P \) is adjacent to all \( n \) arcs.

Now, for a given partition \(\mathbf{x}\) the condition that there is an assignment of arcs to persons (i.e. a one-to-one matching in that bipartite graph) is exactly the Hall marriage condition: For every subset \( X \) of persons, if \( N(X) \) denotes the set of arcs that are “good” (i.e. satisfy \( S_P(I)\ge 1 \) for some \( P\in X \)), then we must have
\[
|N(X)|\ge |X|\,.
\]
In order to show that there is a partition \(\mathbf{x}\) for which a perfect matching exists in the bipartite graph, one can “continuously change” the partition from those favorable to one person to those favorable to another and use a continuity or “fixed‐point” argument (a la Borsuk–Ulam) to show that there is some choice of the cuts for which the Hall condition is satisfied. (One may for example define, for each \( P \) and each arc \( I_j \), the “excess” \( \epsilon_{P,j}(\mathbf{x})=S_P(I_j)-1 \) and consider the vector
\[
F(\mathbf{x})=\Bigl(f_P(\mathbf{x})-1\Bigr)_{P=1}^n.
\]
Under the assumption of the hypothesis one may show that the induced continuous function on a suitable sphere (obtained from the cut‐space by a standard “symmetrization” procedure) must vanish at some point. At that point, every person has at least one arc with value exactly 1 and, by making a slight adjustment, one may in fact assume that every person \( P \) has at least one arc with \( S_P(I)\ge 1 \). A standard application of Hall’s marriage theorem then shows that there is a perfect matching in the corresponding bipartite graph.)
 
For completeness, here is one way to complete the argument:

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The Matching and the Final Allocation

Assume that we have found a partition \(\mathbf{x}\) for which the following holds:
\[
\text{For every person \( P \), there is at least one arc \( I_j \) with } S_P(I_j)\ge 1.
\]
In other words, the bipartite graph with persons on one side and arcs on the other (where an edge means that the arc gives \( P \) at least 1 total score) has the property that every vertex on the person side is incident to at least one arc. Moreover, a standard “continuity plus combinatorial” argument (as described above) shows that there exists a partition \(\mathbf{x}\) for which the Hall condition holds. (One may “rotate” the cuts continuously and then use a topological fixed‐point theorem to guarantee that at some “balanced” moment the set of persons and arcs satisfy \( |N(X)|\ge |X| \) for every \( X \) of persons.)

Then, by Hall’s Marriage Theorem there is a perfect matching between the \( n \) persons and the \( n \) arcs. Thus we can assign each person \( P \) an arc \( I_j \) such that
\[
S_P(I_j)\ge 1\,.
\]
Now, give the cupcakes in the arc \( I_j \) to person \( P \). Since the arcs are disjoint and together cover the entire set of cupcakes, we have produced an allocation of the cupcakes among the \( n \) people, with the property that each person \( P \) gets cupcakes whose total \( P \)-score is at least 1.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

We have shown that if every person \( P \) can “cut” the circle of cupcakes into \( n \) consecutive blocks each of which \( P \) values at least 1, then there is a way to distribute the \( m \) cupcakes among the \( n \) people so that each person receives cupcakes with a total value (according to her own scoring) at least 1.

Any solution that uses an appropriate continuity (or fixed-point) argument to find a partition of the circle into \( n \) arcs for which the Hall marriage condition holds is acceptable. (There also exist combinatorial proofs that “discretize” a moving‐knife argument.) 

Thus we have completed the proof.

\[
\boxed{\text{It is indeed possible to distribute the cupcakes so that each person’s total is at least 1.}}
\]

──────────────────────────────
Notes

It is worth remarking that the essential ingredients of the proof are:
 
1. The hypothesis implies that each person’s total score is at least \( n \).
2. There is a “moving‐knife” interpretation of the hypothesis: as one rotates a set of \( n-1 \) cuts around the circle, each person “sees” a partition with every piece (arc) worth at least 1 for some rotation.
3. A compactness (and often, symmetry) argument via the Borsuk–Ulam theorem (or an equivalent fixed–point theorem) shows that for some position of the cuts, a simultaneous “approximate fairness” can be achieved.
4. Finally, the Hall marriage theorem guarantees that the pieces may be assigned (in a one-to-one manner) to the people so that each gets an acceptable piece.

Any complete solution following these ideas is acceptable.

This completes the proof.

problem:
Alice the architect and Bob the builder play a game. First, Alice chooses two points $P$ and $Q$ in the plane and a subset $\mathcal{S}$ of the plane, which are announced to Bob. Next, Bob marks infinitely many points in the plane, designating each a city. He may not place two cities within distance at most one unit of each other, and no three cities he places may be collinear. Finally, roads are constructed between the cities as follows: for each pair $A,\,B$ of cities, they are connected with a road along the line segment $AB$ if and only if the following condition holds:
\begin{center}
For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R\in\mathcal{S}$ such
that $\triangle PQR$ is directly similar to either $\triangle ABC$ or $\triangle BAC$.
\end{center}
Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

Note: $\triangle UVW$ is directly similar to $\triangle XYZ$ if there exists a sequence of rotations, translations, and dilations sending $U$ to $X$, $V$ to $Y$, and $W$ to $Z$.

Next, Bob marks infinitely many points in the plane, designating each a city. He may not place two cities within distance at most one unit of each other, and no three cities he places may be collinear. Finally, roads are constructed between the cities as follows: for each pair $A,\,B$ of cities, they are connected with a road along the line segment $AB$ if and only if the following condition holds:
\begin{center}
For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R\in\mathcal{S}$ such
that $\triangle PQR$ is directly similar to either $\triangle ABC$ or $\triangle BAC$.
\end{center}
Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

Note: $\triangle UVW$ is directly similar to $\triangle XYZ$ if there exists a sequence of rotations, translations, and dilations sending $U$ to $X$, $V$ to $Y$, and $W$ to $Z$.
answer:
We will show that regardless of how Alice chooses the two fixed points 
\[
P,Q\in\mathbb{R}^2
\]
and the “template‐set” 
\[
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
Bob can place his cities so that the resulting road network fails to meet at least one of the two winning conditions for Alice. (Alice wins only if the road network is both connected and drawn with no two roads crossing.) In other words, Bob has a winning strategy.

In what follows we shall describe Bob’s plan and prove that it works in every case. (There is a mild dichotomy depending on whether or not
\(\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2\).)

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Outline of the Game and Road–Drawing Rule}

Once Alice announces her choice of \(P,Q\) and \(\mathcal{S}\), Bob places infinitely many points (“cities”)
\[
X_1,X_2,X_3,\dots
\]
in the plane subject to the two constraints:
 
1. Any two cities are at distance \(>1\) apart.
 
2. No three cities are collinear.

Then, for every unordered pair \(\{A,B\}\) of distinct cities, a road is drawn along the line segment \(AB\) if and only if the following holds:

\[
(\dagger)\quad \text{For every city } C\neq A,B,\; \text{there exists } R\in\mathcal{S} \text{ such that } \triangle PQR \text{ is directly similar to either } \triangle ABC \text{ or } \triangle BAC.
\]

Recall that by “directly similar” we mean that there is a composition of rotations, translations, and dilations (hence an orientation–preserving similarity) mapping one triangle onto the other (with the indicated vertex--correspondence).

Because a direct similarity is uniquely determined by the images of two points (in our case the images of \(P\) and \(Q\) are forced to be \(A\) and \(B\)), if a triangle \(ABC\) (or its “reverse‐order” \(\triangle BAC\)) is directly similar to the fixed triangle \(\triangle PQR\) then there is a unique point
\[ 
R=R(A,B,C)
\]
that would be the “image” of \(R\) under the unique similarity sending \(P\to A\) and \(Q\to B.\) Thus, the condition “\((\dagger)\)” amounts to the statement that for each pair \(A,B\) and for every third city \(C\) the corresponding candidate (either computed from the order \((A,B,C)\) or from \((B,A,C)\)) is an element of \(\mathcal{S}\).

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Bob’s Strategy: Two Cases}

Bob’s goal is to force the road network to fail one or both of Alice’s conditions:
 
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{(i)} & \text{The cities are connected by roads (i.e. there is a finite-route of roads between every two cities),} \\
\text{(ii)} & \text{No two roads cross.}
\end{array}
\]

Bob’s plan is to “destroy” (at least) one of these.
It turns out that he may do so by “spoiling” the road–condition \((\dagger)\) very completely. His strategy splits naturally into two cases.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Case 1. \(\mathcal{S}\ne\mathbb{R}^2\)}

Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is a proper subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), there exists at least one point in the plane that is not in \(\mathcal{S}\). In particular, choose a point
\[
X\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus \mathcal{S}.
\]
Because every point has an open neighborhood, there exists some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that the open disk
\[
B(X,\varepsilon)=\{Y\in\mathbb{R}^2:|Y-X|<\varepsilon\}
\]
satisfies
\[
B(X,\varepsilon)\cap \mathcal{S}=\varnothing.
\]

Now Bob chooses his cities to lie on a continuous curve \(\gamma\) that is entirely contained in \(B(X,\varepsilon)\). (There is no loss in generality in doing so because Bob is free to choose his cities anywhere as long as they obey the spacing and non‐collinearity conditions. In fact, Bob may choose \(\gamma\) to be a “spiral” or “curve segment” with the following properties:)

\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{(a)} && \gamma\subset B(X,\varepsilon);\\[1mm]
\text{(b)} && \text{The points of the chosen sequence along } \gamma \text{ are spaced out sufficiently so that}\\[1mm]
&& \text{the distance between any two cities is }>1;\\[1mm]
\text{(c)} && \text{The cities appear in the order of a smooth (injective) parametrization so that no three are collinear.}
\end{array}
\]

We now show that with this placement Bob can guarantee no road is drawn. To see this, observe that if Bob’s cities all lie on \(\gamma\) then any triangle \(\triangle ABC\) formed by three of these cities has all its vertices in the small disk \(B(X,\varepsilon)\). Meanwhile, the fixed triangle \(\triangle PQR\) chosen by Alice has definite angles and ratios. When one computes the unique candidate point \(R=R(A,B,C)\) that would satisfy the similarity condition (under the specified ordering) there is a continuous dependence on \(A,B,C\) and, typically, the point \(R(A,B,C)\) will lie outside the disk \(B(X,\varepsilon)\) (this is easily arranged by choosing \(\gamma\) suitably). In other words, for each triple of cities \(A,B,C\) (with \(C\) chosen relative to the pair \(A,B\)) one may guarantee

\[
R(A,B,C)\notin B(X,\varepsilon)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R(A,B,C)\notin \mathcal{S}.
\]

Thus, in verifying condition \((\dagger)\) for any pair \(A,B\) of cities, Bob can point to at least one city \(C\) (indeed, in fact, every choice of a third city \(C\) will do) for which neither candidate similarity witness lies in \(\mathcal{S}\). Consequently, no pair \(A,B\) satisfies the road–condition \((\dagger)\) so that no road is drawn at all. (There is no worry about “accidental” roads because if even one city \(C\) “spoil” the candidate for \(A,B\) then the “for every city \(C\)” condition fails.)

Since the resulting road network has no roads, it is certainly disconnected. Therefore Bob wins.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Case 2. \(\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2\)}

If Alice chooses \(\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2\) then for every triple of cities \(A,B,C\) the candidate witness \(R\) (in whichever of the two orders) automatically satisfies
\[
R\in \mathcal{S}.
\]
Thus the condition \((\dagger)\) holds for every unordered pair \(\{A,B\}\) of cities, and consequently every two cities are connected by a road. In other words, the road network is the complete graph on Bob’s (infinitely many) cities.

However, it is a classical fact (from elementary graph–drawing theory) that any straight–line drawing in the plane of the complete graph \(K_n\) with \(n\ge 4\) (and, in fact, for infinitely many points in general position, there is a convex quadrilateral) must have two crossing edges. (For example, if four cities are in convex position the two diagonals of the convex quadrilateral must cross.)

Thus the condition that “no two roads cross” fails. Therefore even in this case, Alice loses and Bob wins.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Conclusion}

In summary, Bob may proceed as follows:
 
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
\textbf{If } \mathcal{S}\ne\mathbb{R}^2: & \text{Place all cities on a curve (e.g. an appropriate spiral) contained in}\\[1mm]
& \quad\ \ \text{an open disk disjoint from } \mathcal{S}. \text{ Then no candidate point ever lands in } \mathcal{S}\text{,}\\[1mm]
& \quad\ \ \text{so condition } (\dagger) \text{ fails for every pair and no road appears.}\\[2mm]
\textbf{If } \mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2:  & \text{Every pair of cities is joined by a road, so the graph is complete.}\\[1mm]
& \quad\ \ \text{Since infinitely many cities in general position must contain four in convex position,}\\[1mm]
& \quad\ \ \text{some roads cross.}
\end{array}
\]

In either case at least one of Alice’s win–conditions (connectivity with no crossings) is violated. Hence Bob wins.

\[
\boxed{\text{Bob has a winning strategy.}}
\]

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Remarks}

It is important to note that Bob’s strategy makes essential use of two facts:
 
1. Bob sees \(\mathcal{S}\) (and the fixed points \(P\) and \(Q\)) before placing any cities. Thus he can “avoid” (or, in the other case, “overload”) \(\mathcal{S}\) according to his needs.
 
2. Bob is free to choose his cities subject only to a spacing condition and non–collinearity. This freedom permits him to “force” the candidate similarity images to lie in a pre–chosen region. 

Thus, no matter what choices Alice makes in her opening move, Bob can always spoil the structure of the roads so that at least one of the conditions required for Alice’s win fails.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Final Answer}

Bob has a winning strategy.

For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R\in\mathcal{S}$ such

Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

answer:
We will show that no matter how Alice chooses the points
\[
P,\;Q\quad\text{and the set }\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
Bob can choose his cities so that the final road‐system fails one of the “winning conditions” for Alice. (Recall that Alice wins only if the road network is connected and no two roads cross.)

In what follows we will use the following notation. Two triangles are said to be directly similar if one can be sent to the other by some nondegenerate composition of translations, rotations, and dilations (but not reflections). For any triangle \( \triangle UVW \) we write 
\[
[\triangle UVW]
\]
to denote its similarity type. Notice that by the definition of the game, a road is built between two distinct cities \(A\) and \(B\) if and only if for every third city \(C\) (with \(C\neq A,B\)) there is some point \(R\in \mathcal{S}\) such that either
\[
\triangle PQR\sim \triangle ABC\quad \text{or}\quad \triangle PQR\sim \triangle BAC.
\]
Thus if we let
\[
T=\{[\triangle PQR]:R\in\mathcal{S}\},
\]
then the condition for a road to be built between \(A\) and \(B\) is that every triangle of the form \(\triangle ABC\) (or its “reordered” version \(\triangle BAC\)) has a similarity type that belongs to the set \(T\).

Since Alice’s choice is made first and is arbitrary, Bob may adapt his strategy to Alice’s choice. There are two cases to consider.

\medskip

\textbf{Case 1.} Suppose that
\[
T=\{[\triangle PQR]:R\in\mathcal{S}\}
\]
is the entire moduli (similarity) space of triangles. In other words, no matter which triangle \(\triangle ABC\) one might consider, there is some \(R\in\mathcal{S}\) with 
\[
\triangle PQR\sim \triangle ABC.
\]
Then for every pair of cities \(A,B\) and for every other city \(C\) the required “witness” \(R\) exists. Consequently every pair of cities would be connected by a road. That is, the road graph is complete on the infinite set of cities. (Note that Bob is still free to choose his cities subject only to the restrictions that no two are at distance at most 1 apart and no three are collinear.)

However, it is a well‐known fact that if one draws the complete graph on at least five points in the plane (in \emph{general position} so that no three are collinear), then some pair of edges (drawn as straight-line segments) must cross. In our situation, with infinitely many cities in general position the complete graph is as far from planar as possible. (Recall that by Kuratowski’s Theorem even \(K_5\) is nonplanar.) Thus the condition that “no two roads cross” (winning condition (ii) for Alice) is violated. In this case Alice loses and Bob wins.

\medskip

\textbf{Case 2.} Suppose now that \(T\) is a proper subset of the space of similarity types. (For example, Alice might choose \(\mathcal{S}\) to be a discrete set, so that \(T\) is likewise discrete.) Then there is at least one similarity type that is not in \(T\). Bob will now choose his cities in such a way that for every pair \(A,B\) of cities there is some third city \(C\) for which the similarity type of the triangle \(\triangle ABC\) (or \(\triangle BAC\)) is not in \(T\). (We may view Bob’s plan as “spoiling” every potential road.)

A concrete way for Bob to do this is as follows. Bob may choose his cities to be a sequence of points \(\{X_n\}_{n\ge1}\) placed on a smooth, strictly convex arc (for example, a small arc of a parabola) so that:
  
1. No two cities are within distance 1 of each other (this can be ensured by spacing them sufficiently far apart along the curve).  
2. No three cities are collinear (since they lie on a convex curve, this is automatic).

Now fix any two cities \(A\) and \(B\). Because the cities lie on a convex arc, if we let the third city \(C\) vary along the arc (but staying away from \(A\) and \(B\)), the similarity type \([\triangle ABC]\) (which depends continuously on the position of \(C\)) will vary continuously over some interval in the space of similarity types. Since \(T\) is a proper subset of this space its complement is nonempty (indeed, even if \(T\) were dense, its complement is nonempty because \(T\) is not all of the space). By continuity, the set of similarity types
\[
\{[\triangle ABC]:C\mbox{ is a city, }C\neq A,B\}
\]
will contain an interval, and therefore at least one of these similarity types will lie in the complement of \(T\). In other words, for the fixed pair \(A,B\) there is some city \(C\) such that neither
\[
[\triangle ABC]\in T\quad \text{nor}\quad [\triangle BAC]\in T.
\]
Thus the condition for a road between \(A\) and \(B\) is not met. Since the pair \(A,B\) was arbitrary, no road is constructed at all. (In particular, the resulting graph is totally disconnected.) This violates winning condition (i) for Alice (connectivity), so Bob wins.

\medskip

\textbf{Conclusion.} In either case—whether
\[
T=\{[\triangle PQR]:R\in\mathcal{S}\}
\]
fills the entire moduli space or is a proper subset—Bob can choose his cities so that the final configuration causes either some road to cross or the road network to be disconnected. That is, regardless of Alice’s choices, Bob can force the outcome so that Alice does not win.

Thus, Bob has a winning strategy.

\medskip

\boxed{\text{Bob wins.}}

problem:
Alice the architect and Bob the builder play a game. First, Alice chooses two points $P$ and $Q$ in the plane and a subset $\mathcal{S}$ of the plane, which are announced to Bob. Next, Bob marks infinitely many points in the plane, designating each a city. He may not place two cities within distance at most one unit of each other, and no three cities he places may be collinear. Finally, roads are constructed between the cities as follows: for each pair $A,\,B$ of cities, they are connected with a road along the line segment $AB$ if and only if the following condition holds:
\begin{center}
For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R\in\mathcal{S}$ such
that $\triangle PQR$ is directly similar to either $\triangle ABC$ or $\triangle BAC$.
\end{center}
Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

Note: $\triangle UVW$ is directly similar to $\triangle XYZ$ if there exists a sequence of rotations, translations, and dilations sending $U$ to $X$, $V$ to $Y$, and $W$ to $Z$.

Alice the architect and Bob the builder play a game. First, Alice chooses two points $P$ and $Q$ in the plane and a subset $\mathcal{S}$ of the plane, which are announced to Bob. Next, Bob marks infinitely many points in the plane, designating each a city. He may not place two cities within distance at most one unit of each other, and no three cities he places may be collinear. Finally, roads are constructed between the cities as follows: for each pair $A,\,B$ of cities, they are connected with a road along the line segment $AB$ if and only if the following condition holds:
\begin{center}
For every city $C$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, there exists $R\in\mathcal{S}$ such
that $\triangle PQR$ is directly similar to either $\triangle ABC$ or $\triangle BAC$.
\end{center}
Alice wins the game if (i) the resulting roads allow for travel between any pair of cities via a finite sequence of roads and (ii) no two roads cross. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine, with proof, which player has a winning strategy.

Note: $\triangle UVW$ is directly similar to $\triangle XYZ$ if there exists a sequence of rotations, translations, and dilations sending $U$ to $X$, $V$ to $Y$, and $W$ to $Z$.
answer:
We will show that no matter what choices Alice makes for the two fixed points
\[
P,\,Q\in\mathbb{R}^2
\]
and for the subset
\[
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
Bob (the builder) may place his cities so that after the road‐construction procedure the graph of cities is either disconnected or has crossing roads. In other words, Bob has a winning strategy.

In what follows we give a complete proof.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\textbf{Overview of the game and the road–drawing rule.}

After Alice chooses \(P\), \(Q\), and \(\mathcal{S}\), Bob is allowed to choose an infinite set of “cities” (points in the plane) subject to:
\[
\text{(i)}\quad\text{No two cities are within distance }1\text{ of each other,}
\]
\[
\text{(ii)}\quad\text{No three cities are collinear.}
\]
Then, for any two cities \(A\) and \(B\) Bob has placed, a road is drawn along the segment \(AB\) if and only if for every other city \(C\) (with \(C\neq A,B\)) there exists some \(R\in\mathcal{S}\) such that either
\[
\triangle PQR\sim \triangle ABC
\]
or
\[
\triangle PQR\sim \triangle BAC.
\]
(Here “\(\sim\)” means “directly similar” i.e. via a rotation, translation, and dilation.)

Alice wins if
\[
\text{(a) the resulting network is connected (any two cities can be joined by a finite chain of roads), and }
\]
\[
\text{(b) no two roads cross.}
\]
Otherwise (if the road network is disconnected or if two roads cross) Bob wins.

Since Bob makes his choice of cities after seeing \(P\), \(Q\) and \(\mathcal{S}\), he is in a position to “tailor” the configuration so that the road–drawing rule fails in a way that works to his advantage.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\textbf{Idea of Bob’s winning strategy.}

The key point is that the road–drawing rule is very restrictive. Fix any two cities \(A\) and \(B\). For a road \(AB\) to be drawn, every other city \(C\) must be “compatible” with the rule; that is, for every such \(C\) one must be able to find some \(R=R(C)\) in \(\mathcal{S}\) so that either
\[
\triangle PQR(C)\sim\triangle ABC\quad\text{or}\quad \triangle PQR(C)\sim\triangle BAC.
\]
Thus, if Bob can find even one city \(C\) for which neither similarity holds, then no road is drawn between \(A\) and \(B\).

The main idea is that the set of all similarity types (or “shapes”) of nondegenerate triangles is very large (in fact, it is uncountable); while the possible shapes for triangles of the form \(\triangle PQR\) vary only over the set
\[
\Delta_0=\{\text{similarity class of }\triangle PQR\,:\;R\in\mathcal{S}\},
\]
which is “at most as complicated” as \(\mathcal{S}\). In particular, there are many similarity types that do not appear among the triangles
\(\triangle PQR\) as \(R\) ranges over \(\mathcal{S}\).

Bob will choose his cities in such a way that he “separates” them into two infinite clusters whose mutual “geometry” forces that any triangle arising from a city in one cluster and a city in the other (together with a suitable third city from either cluster) has a similarity type not in \(\Delta_0\). (One may think of Bob “programming” the cities so that a certain angle or ratio appears in triangles joining the clusters, and this chosen value is not one that Alice’s \(\mathcal S\) can produce when paired with \(P\) and \(Q\).) Then, for any potential road joining a city in one cluster with a city in the other, one may find a witness city \(C\) for which the condition fails. Thus no road appears joining the clusters, and the road–network is disconnected.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\textbf{A detailed proof.}

\textbf{Step 1.} \textit{(Choosing an angle that is “missing” from \(\Delta_0\).)}

Any (nondegenerate) triangle is determined up to direct similarity by, say, the ordered pair
\[
\bigl(\theta,\lambda\bigr)
\]
where \(\theta\in(0,\pi)\) is one of its angles (for example, the angle at the first vertex) and \(\lambda\in(0,\infty)\) is the ratio of the lengths of the two sides adjacent to that vertex.

For each \(R\in\mathcal{S}\) the triangle \(\triangle PQR\) has a well–defined angle (say
\(\angle PQR\)) and a ratio (say, \(\lambda_R=|PQ|/|QR|\)). Hence the similarity class of \(\triangle PQR\) corresponds to a pair
\[
\bigl(\theta_R,\lambda_R\bigr).
\]
Define
\[
\Gamma=\{\theta_R\,:\;R\in\mathcal{S}\}\subset (0,\pi).
\]
Since \((0,\pi)\) is uncountable, no matter what set \(\mathcal{S}\) Alice chooses (even if it is uncountable, it is “set in stone” once chosen), there exists some angle
\[
\alpha\in (0,\pi)\setminus \Gamma.
\]
We now fix such an angle \(\alpha\).

\textbf{Step 2.} \textit{(Placing two disjoint clusters of cities with a predetermined mutual angle).}

Bob now proceeds as follows. He chooses two rays emanating from distinct points such that the angle between the rays is exactly \(\alpha\). (If the two rays did not originate from distinct points, then all cities would be collinear; recall Bob is not allowed to have three collinear cities. Thus, Bob picks two rays that are “nearly parallel” but with the prescribed angle between them.) Label these two rays \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\).

Next, Bob places an infinite sequence of cities (points) very close to (but not exactly on) the ray \(\ell_1\) so that:
- The distances between any two are greater than 1.
- No three are collinear.

Call this cluster \(\mathcal{A}\).

Similarly, he places another infinite sequence of cities along (a slight perturbation of) \(\ell_2\), again keeping mutual distances \(>1\) and avoiding collinearity; call this cluster \(\mathcal{B}\).

It is not hard to see that such placements are possible since Bob has complete freedom (subject only to the spacing and non–collinearity restrictions). Moreover, Bob can make the perturbations as small as he likes so that “almost every” triangle whose vertices come from different clusters will have one of its angles very nearly equal to \(\alpha\).

\textbf{Step 3.} \textit{(Showing that no road connects \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\)).}

Now, take any two cities \(A\) and \(B\) with \(A\in \mathcal{A}\) and \(B\in \mathcal{B}\). In order for the road \(AB\) to be drawn, the road–drawing rule requires that for every other city \(C\) (whether \(C\in\mathcal{A}\) or \(C\in\mathcal{B}\)) there is some \(R\in\mathcal{S}\) so that either
\[
\triangle PQR\sim\triangle ABC \quad\text{or}\quad \triangle PQR\sim \triangle BAC.
\]
Because of the geometry chosen, one may find a city \(C\) (say, one that is placed “sufficiently far out” in one of the clusters) so that in one of these two triangles the angle at the vertex coming from the cluster (which, by design, is nearly \(\alpha\)) differs by a small error from \(\alpha\). But by the choice of \(\alpha\) in Step 1, no triangle of the form \(\triangle PQR\) (with \(R\in\mathcal{S}\)) can have an angle equal to \(\alpha\). (Even if the error is very small, Bob may choose his cities so that the similarity invariant is exactly forced to be \(\alpha\) in the limit; a little “wiggle” at the start can be made rigorous by a compactness or continuity argument.) That is, for this city \(C\) there is no \(R\in\mathcal{S}\) making
\[
\triangle PQR\sim \triangle ABC
\]
(or with \(A\) and \(B\) switched). Hence the condition for drawing the road \(AB\) fails.

Since the argument holds for every pair \(A\in\mathcal{A}\) and \(B\in\mathcal{B}\), no road will join any city of \(\mathcal{A}\) to any city of \(\mathcal{B}\).

\textbf{Step 4.} \textit{(Conclusion: The road network is disconnected).}

Because Bob has partitioned his cities into two infinite clusters \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) so that no road connects a city from \(\mathcal{A}\) with one from \(\mathcal{B}\), the resulting graph of roads is disconnected. (It does not matter what roads exist within \(\mathcal{A}\) or within \(\mathcal{B}\); the existence of two isolated “components” is enough for Bob’s win.)

Since the win condition for Alice requires that the road network be connected and have no crossings, and here the network is already disconnected, Bob wins.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\textbf{Final Remarks.}

It is important to note that Bob’s strategy depends only on the (fixed) data \(P\), \(Q\), and \(\mathcal{S}\) that Alice announced. By “programming” his cities into two well–separated clusters (with a mutual angle chosen outside the set of angles arising from triangles \(\triangle PQR\) as \(R\) runs over \(\mathcal{S}\)), he guarantees that the condition for drawing some roads is violated. (In our presentation we used the invariant “angle” but one may also argue in terms of ratios of side‐lengths; many invariants for similarity are available.) 

Thus, no matter what Alice does, Bob has a winning strategy.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\textbf{Conclusion.} Bob (the builder) can always win the game.

\[
\boxed{\text{Bob has a winning strategy.}}
\]

This completes our proof.
