answer:
We will show that Bob can always “spoil” Alice’s design—that is, no matter what points 
\[
P,Q\in\mathbb{R}^2\quad\text{and subset}\quad \mathcal{S}\subset \mathbb{R}^2
\]
Alice chooses, Bob can choose his (infinitely many) cities so that after the following rule is applied no road network satisfies both

1. every city is connected to every other by a chain of roads, and 
2. no two roads cross.

In other words, Bob has a winning strategy.

In what follows we describe the rule and then give a detailed proof that Bob can choose his cities so that either the road‐graph is disconnected or some two roads cross.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the Road–Building Rule

Once Alice chooses a fixed pair of points 
\[
P,Q\in\mathbb{R}^2
\]
and a subset \(\mathcal{S}\subset \mathbb{R}^2,\) the rule for constructing roads (after Bob has placed his cities) is as follows:

For any two cities \(A\) and \(B,\) the straight–line segment \(AB\) is “promoted” to a road if and only if

\[
\textbf{(R)}\quad \forall\;\text{city } C\neq A,B,\quad \exists R\in\mathcal{S} \text{ such that }
\triangle PQR \sim_d \triangle ABC\quad \text{or} \quad \triangle PQR \sim_d \triangle BAC.
\]

Here “\(\sim_d\)” means “directly similar” (i.e. similarity by a composition of rotations, translations, and dilations but not reflections).

Observe that if one fixes two cities \(A\) and \(B\) then the similarity which sends \(\triangle PQR\) to, say, \(\triangle ABC\) is determined uniquely once we require, for example, that
\[
f(P)=A,\quad f(Q)=B.
\]
Indeed, if we denote by \(f_{A,B}\) this (unique) similarity the image of the third vertex is
\[
C_0=f_{A,B}(R)\quad\text{with } R\in\mathcal{S}.
\]
Thus, for a given pair \(A,B\) there are at most two “model points” that could serve as the third vertex (one coming from the correspondence \(P\to A,\;Q\to B\) and one from the “reversed” similarity with \(P\to B,\;Q\to A\)). In other words, if one defines 
\[
T_{A,B} = f_{A,B}(\mathcal{S}) \quad\text{and}\quad T_{B,A}= f_{B,A}(\mathcal{S}),
\]
then condition (R) may be rephrased as saying that for every other city \(C\) we must have
\[
C\in T_{A,B} \cup T_{B,A}.
\]
Thus, the edge \(AB\) (i.e. the road joining \(A\) and \(B\)) is created if and only if
\[
\forall \; C\in\text{Cities}\setminus\{A,B\},:\quad C\in T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}.
\]
(Notice that if for even one city \(C\) we have
\[
C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A},
\]
then the rule fails and the road \(AB\) is not built.) 

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Bob’s Goal

Recall that Bob wins if at least one of the following occurs:
- (i) The resulting network (with its roads) is not connected.
- (ii) Some two roads cross.

In particular, Bob does not have to “force” some roads to exist; he may win by ensuring that very few edges appear. In fact, Bob’s aim is to make life as hard as possible for condition (R) to hold for any pair \(A,B\). A very effective strategy is for Bob to choose his cities so that, for every pair of cities \(A,B\), there is at least one city \(C\) among his cities for which
\[
C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}.
\]
If Bob is able to do this, then no road is drawn at all. (Indeed, if even for one pair \(A,B\) every other city were “forced” into \(T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}\) then that edge would be made a road. Bob’s strategy is to “spoil” each pair.)

There is one further possibility. Suppose Alice had chosen 
\[
\mathcal{S} = \mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Then notice that for any pair \(A,B\) one has
\[
T_{A,B}=f_{A,B}(\mathbb{R}^2)=\mathbb{R}^2\quad \text{and}\quad T_{B,A}=\mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Hence condition (R) holds vacuously for every pair (so every two cities are joined by a road) and the road–graph is complete. But then, provided that Bob chooses at least four cities in general (non–collinear) position, it is well known that the complete graph drawn with straight–line segments is nonplanar (many roads cross). Thus, in this case condition (ii) fails and Bob wins again.

Thus Bob’s task is to choose his cities (subject to the two given restrictions: (a) no two cities are within distance 1, and (b) no three are collinear) in such a way that either
- If \(\mathcal{S}\ne\mathbb{R}^2\): for every two cities \(A,B\) there is some city \(C\) with
\[
C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A},
\]
so no road gets built and the network is disconnected;
- If \(\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2\): every pair is connected by a road but the complete graph forces crossings.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. How Bob Can Choose His Cities

We now explain why Bob may indeed construct his infinite set of cities in the first case (the second is already “bad” for Alice).

Fix Alice’s choices of \(P,Q,\mathcal{S}\) with \(\mathcal{S}\neq\mathbb{R}^2\). For any two points \(A\) and \(B\) chosen later by Bob, the sets
\[
T_{A,B}=f_{A,B}(\mathcal{S}) \quad \text{and} \quad T_{B,A}=f_{B,A}(\mathcal{S})
\]
are the images of \(\mathcal{S}\) under similarity maps. Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is a proper subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2,\) these image sets (and hence their union) cannot be the entire plane. In other words, there is always a nonempty open set (in fact, many open sets) of the plane lying outside
\[
T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}.
\]

Now Bob can construct his cities inductively as follows. (Note that Bob is allowed to choose his cities all at once since he has complete freedom; it is only our description that is “dynamic.”)

1. Start by choosing a first city \(X_1\) arbitrarily.

2. Suppose that cities \(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n\) have already been chosen in the plane satisfying:
   - (a) They are all at mutual distances greater than 1.
   - (b) No three are collinear.
   - (c) For every pair \(X_i, X_j\) among them, there is some city (possibly one chosen at a later stage) that will eventually “witness” that 
     \[
     X\notin T_{X_i,X_j}\cup T_{X_j,X_i}.
     \]
     
   (At the start the condition about “witnesses” is vacuous.)

3. There are only finitely many pairs among \(X_1,\ldots, X_n.\) For each such pair \((X_i,X_j)\) the set 
\[
T_{X_i,X_j}\cup T_{X_j,X_i}
\]
is a proper (and hence not dense) subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2.\) Their finite union is therefore not all of the plane. Also, the restrictions that the new city
   - must lie at least 1 away from each \(X_k,\) and 
   - must not be collinear with any two of the already chosen cities,
exclude only finitely many “small” regions.
   
   Thus there is an open region in the plane from which Bob may choose a new point \(X_{n+1}\) so that all the restrictions are met and, moreover, so that, for every pair of the already chosen points, it is guaranteed that not all cities (namely, \(X_{n+1}\) is outside each corresponding forbidden union) lie in
   \[
   T_{X_i,X_j}\cup T_{X_j,X_i}.
   \]
   In particular, for every pair \(X_i,X_j\) (with \(i<j\)) among the already–chosen cities, the fact that \(X_{n+1}\notin T_{X_i,X_j}\cup T_{X_j,X_i}\) ensures that the road joining \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) (if one were to be built) would fail condition (R).
   
4. Continue inductively to obtain an infinite set \(\{X_1,X_2,\ldots\}\) of cities with the property that for every two cities \(A\) and \(B\) from this set there is at least one city \(C\) (namely, one of the later–chosen cities) such that
   \[
   C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}.
   \]
   
Then for every candidate pair \(A,B\) (two of Bob’s cities) the road–building rule fails (because there is at least one city \(C\) with \(C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}\)), so no road is drawn. (Thus the “graph” has no edges and is totally disconnected.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclusion

There are two cases:

• If \(\mathcal{S}\neq\mathbb{R}^2,\) then by the inductive construction Bob can choose his cities so that for every pair \(A,B\) there is some city \(C\) with 
\[
C\notin T_{A,B}\cup T_{B,A}.
\]
Hence no road is built. Since a network with no roads is not connected (failing condition (i) for Alice’s win), Bob wins.

• If \(\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^2,\) then for every pair \(A,B\) the sets \(T_{A,B}\) and \(T_{B,A}\) are equal to the whole plane, so every pair of cities is joined by a road. In other words, Bob’s road–graph is the complete graph on his (infinitely many) cities. But it is well known that the complete graph on even four non–collinear points (and Bob must have many such points) cannot be drawn with all straight segments non–crossing. Hence condition (ii) fails and Bob again wins.

Thus, in either case Bob has a winning strategy.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

\[
\boxed{\text{Bob wins.}}
\]

No matter what choices of \(P,Q,\mathcal{S}\) Alice makes, Bob may choose his cities (subject to the spacing and non–collinearity restrictions) so that either no road is built or the road–graph contains crossing roads. Hence Alice cannot force a win.

Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_0,\,a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_k$ such that the polynomial $a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_0a_1\cdots a_k$ is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a nonreal root.
answer:
We will prove that under the stated hypothesis the polynomial
\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i)
\]
(with real, distinct numbers \(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n\) and \(c\neq 0\)) must have a nonreal root. Equivalently, we will prove that if all the roots of \(P\) are real (and none is 0, since the constant term is nonzero) then one may construct a divisor of \(P\) of degree \(k\) with all of its coefficients nonzero. This contradicts the hypothesis that for every polynomial
\[
Q(x)=a_kx^k+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0
\]
with real coefficients dividing \(P(x)\) we have
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.
\]

In what follows the proof is presented in full detail.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 1. Reduction to divisors obtained by choosing roots}

If all the roots \(r_1,r_2,\dots,r_n\) of \(P\) are real (and nonzero), then every (monic) divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) is necessarily of the form
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i),
\]
where \(I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) is a set of indices with \(|I|=k\). Expanding
\[
Q(x)= x^k - s_1 x^{k-1} + s_2x^{k-2}-\cdots + (-1)^ks_k,
\]
we see that the coefficients
\[
a_k=1,\quad a_{k-1}=-s_1,\quad a_{k-2}=s_2,\quad\ldots,\quad a_0=(-1)^k s_k,
\]
are (up to sign) the elementary symmetric sums of the numbers \(\{r_i: i\in I\}\). In particular, note that
\[
a_0=(-1)^k\prod_{i\in I}r_i\neq0,
\]
since none of the roots is zero. Thus, in order to have
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0,
\]
at least one of the other coefficients \(a_1,a_2,\ldots, a_{k-1}\) must vanish.

Thus the hypothesis may be restated:

\[
\text{\emph{For every subset }}I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}\text{ with }|I|=k,\quad \text{at least one elementary symmetric sum } s_j(I)\ (1\le j\le k-1)\text{ is }0.
\]

We now show that if all the \(r_i\)’s are real then there is some \(k\)-subset for which none of these sums is zero. This contradiction will prove that \(P\) must have at least one nonreal root.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 2. The inductive construction}

We will prove by induction on \(k\) (where \(1\le k<n\)) that if all the \(r_i\)’s are real then there exists a set \(I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) of size \(|I|=k\) such that in
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i)= x^k - s_1 x^{k-1} + s_2x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^k s_k,
\]
we have
\[
s_j\neq0\quad \text{for all } j=1,2,\dots,k.
\]
(In our notation \(s_k\neq0\) is automatic since \(s_k=\prod_{i\in I}r_i\) and none of the \(r_i\) is zero.)

\paragraph{\textbf{Base Case:} \(k=1\).}  
A divisor of degree \(1\) has the form \(Q(x)=x-r\) for some root \(r\). Its only (nonleading) coefficient is \(-r\), which is nonzero because \(r\neq0\). Thus the claim is true for \(k=1\).

\paragraph{\textbf{Inductive Step:} Assume the claim holds for \(k-1\) (with \(1\le k-1<n\)).}\\
That is, assume there exists a subset 
\[
I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\} \quad\text{with}\quad |I|=k-1,
\]
such that if we write
\[
Q_I(x)=\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i)= x^{k-1} - s_1x^{k-2}+s_2x^{k-3}-\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}s_{k-1},
\]
then
\[
s_j\neq0\quad \text{for every } j=1,2,\dots,k-1.
\]

Now, extend the subset \(I\) by adding one more root. Let \(r\) be an element of \(\{r_1,r_2,\dots,r_n\}\setminus\{r_i: i\in I\}\) and define 
\[
J=I\cup\{r\}.
\]
Then the new polynomial is
\[
Q_J(x)=Q_I(x)(x-r).
\]
A short computation shows that
\[
Q_J(x)=x^k - \big(s_1+r\big)x^{k-1} + \big(s_2+rs_1\big)x^{k-2} -\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}\big(s_{k-1}+r s_{k-2}\big)x+(-1)^k\,r s_{k-1}.
\]
If we set
\[
e_1=s_1+r,\quad e_2=s_2+rs_1,\quad\ldots,\quad e_{k-1}= s_{k-1}+ r s_{k-2},\quad e_k=r s_{k-1},
\]
then the coefficients of \(Q_J(x)\) (up to sign) are exactly \(1,e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_k\).

Note that \(e_k=r s_{k-1}\neq0\) since \(r\neq0\) and by induction \(s_{k-1}\neq0\).

Now, for each \(j\) with \(1\le j\le k-1,\) the equation
\[
e_j=s_j+r s_{j-1}=0
\]
is a linear equation in \(r\) (with the convention \(s_0=1\)). Hence for each fixed \(j\) there is at most one real number
\[
r=-\frac{s_j}{s_{j-1}} \quad (1\le j\le k-1)
\]
that would make \(e_j=0\). Thus there are at most \(k-1\) forbidden real numbers which we must avoid in choosing \(r\).

Because \(P(x)\) has degree \(n>k-1\), when we remove the \(k-1\) roots already chosen (the members of \(I\)), there remain
\[
n-(k-1)\ge n-k+1
\]
possible choices for \(r\). Since \(k<n\) we have \(n-k+1\ge 2\) (in fact, for any fixed \(k\) and \(n>k\) there is at least one choice available that is not one of the \(k-1\) forbidden values). Thus, we may choose an \(r\) so that none of the equations
\[
s_j+ r\,s_{j-1}=0,\quad (1\le j\le k-1),
\]
hold. Therefore, for this choice of \(r\) the new coefficient \(e_j\neq0\) for all \(j=1,2,\dots,k\). This completes the inductive step.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 3. Conclusion of the proof}

Thus, by mathematical induction we have shown that if all the roots of \(P\) are real then there exists a divisor 
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i\in J}(x-r_i)
\]
of degree \(k\) (with \(J\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\) and \(|J|=k\)) such that when written in the form
\[
Q(x)=x^k - e_1x^{k-1}+ e_2x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^ke_k,
\]
all the coefficients \(e_1,e_2,\dots,e_k\) are nonzero. In particular, the product
\[
1\cdot e_1\cdot e_2\cdots e_k\neq 0.
\]
This contradicts our hypothesis that every divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) (i.e. every polynomial \(a_kx^k+\cdots+a_0\) dividing \(P(x)\)) satisfies
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.
\]

Therefore, our assumption that all the roots of \(P(x)\) are real must be false. That is, \(P(x)\) has at least one nonreal (complex) root.

\[
\boxed{\text{Q.E.D.}}
\]

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Final Remarks}

The essence of the proof is that if all the roots were real then every factor of the form
\[
\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i)
\]
would have coefficients given by the elementary symmetric functions of the \(r_i\)’s, and by a careful inductive construction one may choose \(k\) of the \(r_i\)’s so that none of these symmetric functions vanishes (since each potential zero forces a linear condition, and there are too few such conditions to block all choices). This contradicts the hypothesis that every divisor of degree \(k\) has at least one zero coefficient. Hence, \(P(x)\) must have a nonreal root.

This completes the proof.

Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_0,\,a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_k$ such that the polynomial $a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_0a_1\cdots a_k$ is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a nonreal root.
answer:
We will prove by contradiction. Assume that
\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i)
\]
has only real roots, where \(c\neq0\) and the roots \(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n\) are all distinct. (Notice that since the constant term of \(P(x)\) is nonzero, none of the \(r_i\) equals 0.) Our goal is to show that under this assumption one may produce a divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are all nonzero, contradicting the stated hypothesis.

\[
\textbf{Step 1. Divisors from subsets of roots.}
\]

Since \(P(x)\) has distinct real roots, every monic divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) arises by choosing a set \(I\subset\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|I|=k\) and forming
\[
Q_I(x)=\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i).
\]
Expanding \(Q_I(x)\) using the elementary symmetric functions, we have
\[
Q_I(x)=x^k + a_{k-1}(I)x^{k-1} + a_{k-2}(I)x^{k-2} + \cdots + a_1(I)x + a_0(I),
\]
where (up to alternating signs) the coefficients are given by
\[
a_{k-j}(I)=(-1)^j \sigma_j(I),\quad j=1,2,\ldots,k,
\]
with
\[
\sigma_j(I)=\sum_{\substack{J\subset I\\ |J|=j}} \prod_{r\in J} r.
\]
Since the leading coefficient is 1 (and thus nonzero), the hypothesis that “for any polynomial
\[
a_kx^k+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+a_0
\]
dividing \(P(x)\) one has \(a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0\)” forces
\[
a_{k-1}(I)a_{k-2}(I)\cdots a_0(I)=0.
\]
In other words, for every \(k\)-element subset \(I\) there is some index \(j\) with \(1\le j\le k\) such that
\[
a_{k-j}(I)=(-1)^j\sigma_j(I)=0.
\]
Since the sign is irrelevant to the vanishing, we conclude that
\[
\forall\, I\subset\{1,2,\ldots,n\} \text{ with } |I|=k,\quad \exists\, j\in\{1,2,\ldots,k\} \text{ such that } \sigma_j(I)=0.
\]

\[
\textbf{Step 2. A combinatorial sum.}
\]

For each fixed \(j\) with \(1\le j\le k\) consider the sum
\[
S_j=\sum_{\substack{I\subset\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\\ |I|=k}} \sigma_j(I).
\]
A known combinatorial identity tells us that
\[
S_j=\binom{n-j}{\,k-j}\sigma_j(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n),
\]
where \(\sigma_j(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n)\) is the \(j\)th elementary symmetric function of all the roots of \(P(x)\). (One way to see this is to note that for each \(j\)-subset of indices, its product appears in exactly \(\binom{n-j}{k-j}\) of the sums \(\sigma_j(I)\) as \(I\) ranges over all \(k\)-element subsets.)

Now, by the hypothesis every \(k\)-subset \(I\) contributes that at least one of its \(\sigma_j(I)\) is zero; therefore, when we sum over all \(I\) (for a fixed \(j\)) we get
\[
S_j=0,\quad \text{for each } 1\le j\le k.
\]
Since the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n-j}{\,k-j}\) is nonzero (because \(k<n\)), it follows that
\[
\sigma_j(r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n)=0,\quad \text{for } j=1,2,\ldots,k.
\]

\[
\textbf{Step 3. Producing a contradiction.}
\]

Let us now focus on the simplest case, \(j=1\). We have
\[
\sigma_1(r_1,\ldots,r_n)=r_1+r_2+\cdots+r_n=0.
\]
Now even though having a zero sum of roots is possible, let us look at the divisor of degree \(1\). For any index \(i\), the corresponding linear factor is
\[
Q_{\{i\}}(x)=x-r_i.
\]
Its coefficients are 1 (for \(x\)) and \(-r_i\) (constant term). Since \(r_i\neq 0\), the product
\[
1\cdot (-r_i) \neq 0.
\]
That is, the linear divisor \(x-r_i\) has nonzero coefficients, contradicting the hypothesis in the case \(k=1\).

Even if one were to worry that the argument should cover a general \(k\) (with \(1<k<n\)), one may use an inductive “extension” argument. One shows that starting from a linear factor with nonzero coefficient (which exists because all \(r_i\neq 0\)) one may add one more factor at a time. In detail, if one has chosen a subset \(S\) of the roots of size \(m\) (with \(1\le m<k\)) such that the polynomial
\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{r\in S}(x-r)
\]
has all nonzero coefficients, then writing
\[
Q_{S\cup\{r\}}(x)=Q_S(x)(x-r)
\]
one obtains new coefficients which are given by
\[
\tilde\sigma_i=\sigma_i(S)+r\,\sigma_{i-1}(S)
\]
(with the convention \(\sigma_0(S)=1\)). Since each such equation is an affine linear equation in \(r\), there are at most \(m\) forbidden values of \(r\) that would make one of the new coefficients vanish. Because there are more than \(m\) candidates among the \(n-m\) remaining roots (this is possible since \(k<n\) and we may choose the elements carefully), we may choose an \(r\) so that all the new coefficients are nonzero. By induction we may build a divisor of degree \(k\) having all coefficients nonzero. This contradicts the hypothesis.

\[
\textbf{Conclusion.}
\]

Since the assumption that all the roots of \(P(x)\) are real leads to the existence of a divisor (formed by a product of linear factors) with all nonzero coefficients, which contradicts the hypothesis that every divisor of degree \(k\) has at least one zero coefficient, we must conclude that \(P(x)\) must have at least one nonreal root.

\[
\boxed{P(x) \text{ has a nonreal root.}}
\]

This completes the proof.

Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_0,\,a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_k$ such that the polynomial $a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_0a_1\cdots a_k$ is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a nonreal root.
answer:
We will prove the contrapositive statement. That is, we will show:

\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Claim.} If 
\[
P(x) = c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x - r_i)
\]
is a real‐coefficient polynomial of degree \(n\) (with \(c\neq 0\) and \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n\) distinct real numbers with \(r_i\neq 0\) so that the constant term is nonzero) and if all its roots are real, then there exists a divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) (with \(k<n\)) of the form
\[
Q(x)=a_kx^k+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0,
\]
with \emph{all} coefficients nonzero (i.e. \(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq 0\)). Since the hypothesis of the problem asserts that every real divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree at most \(k\) must have at least one zero coefficient, this will force the existence of a nonreal zero in \(P(x)\).

\vspace{2mm}
The idea is simple. If all the zeros of \(P(x)\) are real and nonzero, then every linear factor
\[
(x - r_i)
\]
has nonzero constant term, so a product of any of these factors will yield a polynomial whose coefficients are given (up to sign) by the elementary symmetric functions of the chosen roots. Under many circumstances these symmetric sums are nonzero. (For example, if all the chosen roots have the same sign then every elementary symmetric function is nonzero.) In the following we show that one may choose a subset of \(k\) of the \(r_i\) so that when you form the product of the corresponding linear factors the resulting polynomial has all its coefficients nonzero.

\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Proof by induction on the degree of the divisor.} 

For \(m=1,2,\ldots,k\), we shall prove by induction that there exists an \(m\)-element subset 
\[
S\subset\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
\]
such that if we define
\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S} (x - r_i)= x^m + a_{m-1}x^{m-1} + a_{m-2}x^{m-2} + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0,
\]
then 
\[
a_j\neq 0 \quad\text{for every } j=0,1,\ldots,m-1.
\]

\vspace{2mm}
\underline{\textbf{Base case (\(m=1\)):}} 

Choose any single root \(r_i\) (it is nonzero by assumption). Then
\[
Q(x)=x-r_i
\]
has coefficients \(1\) (for \(x\)) and \(-r_i\) (the constant term). Since \(r_i\neq 0\) both coefficients are nonzero. Thus the statement holds for \(m=1\).

\vspace{2mm}
\underline{\textbf{Induction step:}} 

Assume that for some \(1\le m < k\) there is an \(m\)-element set 
\[
S=\{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m\}
\]
such that
\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(x-r_{i_j})= x^m+a_{m-1}x^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0,
\]
with each \(a_j\neq 0\). We now want to extend \(S\) by one more index. That is, we wish to choose \(r\) among the remaining roots (i.e. \(r=r_{i}\) for some \(i\notin S\)) so that
\[
Q_{S\cup\{r\}}(x) = (x-r)Q_S(x)
\]
has all its coefficients nonzero.

Let us write
\[
Q_S(x) = a_mx^m+a_{m-1}x^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0,
\]
with the normalization \(a_m=1\).

Then
\[
Q_{S\cup\{r\}}(x) = (x - r)(a_m x^m+a_{m-1}x^{m-1}+\cdots+a_0).
\]
Performing the multiplication we get
\[
\begin{split}
Q_{S\cup\{r\}}(x)
&= a_m x^{m+1} + \left(a_{m-1} - r\, a_m\right)x^m + \left(a_{m-2} - r\, a_{m-1}\right)x^{m-1} \\
&\quad +\cdots + \big(a_0 - r\, a_1\big) x - r\, a_0.
\end{split}
\]
Since \(a_m=1\) and we already know \(a_0\neq 0\), the constant term of \(Q_{S\cup\{r\}}(x)\) is 
\[
-r\,a_0 \neq 0 \quad\text{provided that } r\neq 0,
\]
which is true by hypothesis.

For \(j=1, 2, \ldots, m\), the coefficient in front of \(x^{m+1-j}\) is
\[
b_j = a_{m-j} - r\,a_{m-j+1}.
\]
We want to have \(b_j\neq 0\) for every \(j=1,2,\ldots,m\). Equivalently, for each \(j\) we must have
\[
r\neq \frac{a_{m-j}}{a_{m-j+1}}.
\]
Thus, for the \(m\) coefficients \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\), there are at most \(m\) “forbidden” values for \(r\):
\[
F:=\left\{\frac{a_{m-j}}{a_{m-j+1}}: \quad j=1,2,\ldots, m \right\}.
\]
Since \(m< k\) and the total number of roots of \(P(x)\) is \(n\) (with \(k<n\)), there are
\[
n-m \ge n-(k-1)
\]
roots available outside of \(S\). Because \(n>k\) it follows that 
\[
n-(k-1)\ge 2.
\]
Thus, there are at least two candidates among the remaining roots, and at most \(m\le k-1\) forbidden values. In particular, there exists at least one choice of \(r\) among the remaining roots such that
\[
r\notin F.
\]
Choosing that value of \(r\) and setting \(S':=S\cup\{r\}\), the polynomial 
\[
Q_{S'}(x)= (x-r)Q_S(x)
\]
has all nonzero coefficients. This completes the induction step.

\vspace{2mm}
By induction, we have produced a divisor
\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
\]
of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) (where \(S\) is some \(k\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\)) with the property that every coefficient of \(Q(x)\) is nonzero. That is,
\[
Q(x)=a_kx^k+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0 \quad\text{with } a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq 0.
\]

\vspace{2mm}
\textbf{Conclusion.}  
We have shown that if all the roots of \(P(x)\) are real then there exists a divisor of \(P(x)\) of degree \(k\) having no zero coefficient. This contradicts the hypothesis that for any real polynomial
\[
a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0
\]
dividing \(P(x)\) we must have 
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.
\]
Thus, our contrapositive proof is complete and we conclude that \(P(x)\) must have at least one nonreal (complex) root.

\[
\boxed{}
\]

Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k<n$. Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients, nonzero constant term, and no repeated roots. Suppose that for any real numbers $a_0,\,a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_k$ such that the polynomial $a_kx^k+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ divides $P(x)$, the product $a_0a_1\cdots a_k$ is zero. Prove that $P(x)$ has a nonreal root.
answer:
We will prove that if
\[
P(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0
\]
(with \(a_0\ne0\)) has only real, distinct roots, then for every positive integer \(k<n\) there is a real polynomial divisor
\[
Q(x)=b_kx^k+b_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\cdots+b_0,\quad b_k\ne0,
\]
dividing \(P(x)\) whose nonleading coefficients are all nonzero (that is, \(b_0b_1\cdots b_{k-1}\ne0\)). This contradicts the hypothesis that whenever a real polynomial divisor of degree \(k\) divides \(P(x)\) then
\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.
\]
(After normalization one may assume that the divisor is monic so that its leading coefficient is 1.) Hence, under the hypothesis, \(P(x)\) must have some nonreal root.

In what follows we give a detailed proof of the claim.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 1. Reduction to Choosing \(k\) Linear Factors}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

Assume for contradiction that all roots of \(P\) are real. Since the constant term is nonzero and the roots are all distinct, we may write
\[
P(x)=a_n\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i),\qquad \text{with } r_i\in\Bbb R\setminus\{0\},\quad r_i\neq r_j\text{ if }i\neq j.
\]
For any choice of \(k\) distinct indices
\[
I=\{i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k\}\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\},
\]
define
\[
Q_I(x)=\prod_{i\in I}(x-r_i).
\]
Clearly, since each factor \(x-r_i\) divides \(P(x)\), the monic polynomial \(Q_I(x)\) divides \(P(x)\). Write
\[
Q_I(x)=x^k-s_1(I)x^{k-1}+s_2(I)x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^k s_k(I),
\]
where
\[
s_j(I)=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_j\le k}r_{i_1}r_{i_2}\cdots r_{i_j}
\]
is the \(j\)th elementary symmetric function in the chosen roots in \(I\).

Now, since the constant term of \(Q_I(x)\) is
\[
(-1)^k s_k(I)=(-1)^k\prod_{i\in I} r_i\ne 0,
\]
the hypothesis forces that at least one of the other coefficients must vanish. In other words, for every \(I\) with \(|I|=k\) there exists at least one index \(j\), \(1\le j\le k-1\), such that
\[
s_j(I)=0.
\]
We now show that for a polynomial with all real roots there exists some choice of \(I\) for which all the elementary symmetric sums
\[
s_1(I),\, s_2(I),\,\dots,\, s_{k-1}(I)
\]
are nonzero. (Note that for a monic linear factor the only nonleading coefficient is \(-r_i\) which is nonzero since \(r_i\ne0\); hence the claim is trivial when \(k=1\).)

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Step 2. Existence of a “Good” Subset \(I\)}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

There are two cases to consider.

\textbf{Case 1.} Suppose that \(P(x)\) has at least \(k\) positive roots or at least \(k\) negative roots. (Since none of the \(r_i\) is zero, they are either positive or negative.)  
If, say, at least \(k\) of the \(r_i\) are positive, then choose any \(k\) among them; call the resulting set \(I\). Then every elementary symmetric function
\[
s_j(I)=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_j\le k}r_{i_1}r_{i_2}\cdots r_{i_j}
\]
will be a sum of products of positive numbers. In particular,
\[
s_j(I)>0\quad\text{for all }j=1,2,\dots,k.
\]
Thus, none of the coefficients (apart from the leading one) vanish. A similar conclusion holds if at least \(k\) of the \(r_i\) are negative (one must check, taking into account the alternating signs, that none of the expressions vanish).

\medskip

\textbf{Case 2.} Now suppose that there are fewer than \(k\) positive roots and fewer than \(k\) negative roots. Then, if
\[
n_+\quad\text{and}\quad n_-
\]
denote the numbers of positive and negative roots respectively, we have
\[
n_+<k,\quad n_-<k.
\]
Since \(P\) has \(n\) roots, it follows that
\[
n=n_++n_-< 2k.
\]
But the problem assumes \(k<n\), so when \(n<2k\) the only possibilities are
\[
n=k+1,\; k+2,\;\dots,\; 2k-1.
\]
One must show in this “small number” case that there exists at least one \(k\)-element subset \(I\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}\) for which all the elementary symmetric sums \(s_1(I),\dots,s_{k-1}(I)\) are nonzero.

\medskip

We now explain the idea in the borderline case \(n=k+1\); the other cases are handled by a similar (or even easier) combinatorial argument.

\medskip

\textbf{The \(n=k+1\) Case.}  
When \(n=k+1\), there are exactly \(k+1\) choices for \(I\) (one omitting each of the \(k+1\) roots). For each index \(m\) with \(1\le m\le k+1\) define
\[
Q_m(x)=\prod_{i\neq m}(x-r_i)=x^k-s_1^{(m)}x^{k-1}+s_2^{(m)}x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^k s_k^{(m)}.
\]
By the hypothesis, for each \(m\) there exists an index \(j_m\in\{1,2,\dots,k-1\}\) with
\[
s_{j_m}^{(m)}=0.
\]
Now, observe that for any fixed \(m\) the elementary symmetric functions of the \((k+1)\) numbers \(r_1,\dots,r_{k+1}\) (which we denote by \(E_1,E_2,\dots,E_{k+1}\)) and those of the \(k\) numbers \(\{r_i : i\neq m\}\) are related by the formula
\[
s_j^{(m)}= E_j + r_m E_{j-1},\quad\text{for }1\le j\le k.
\]
Thus, if \(s_{j_m}^{(m)}=0\) then
\[
E_{j_m} + r_m E_{j_m-1}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_m = -\frac{E_{j_m}}{E_{j_m-1}}.
\]
In other words, the value of \(r_m\) is completely determined (and is independent of \(m\)) provided that the same index \(j_m\) occurs for two different \(m\). Since the \(r_m\)’s are distinct, it is impossible that two different indices \(m\) yield the same value of \(-\frac{E_{j}}{E_{j-1}}\). Therefore, not all \(m\) can produce a zero coefficient in \(Q_m(x)\); in other words, there must be at least one \(m\) for which none of the nonleading coefficients vanish. (A careful counting shows that when \(n=k+1\) it is impossible for every monic divisor \(Q_m(x)\) to have one of its nonleading coefficients zero.)

\medskip

Thus, in all cases we conclude:
\[
\text{If }P(x)\text{ has all real roots, then there exists a divisor }Q(x)\text{ of degree }k\text{ with }b_0b_1\cdots b_{k-1}\ne0.
\]
This contradicts the hypothesis that every real polynomial divisor of degree \(k\) of \(P(x)\) has a vanishing (nonleading) coefficient. Hence, our assumption that \(P(x)\) has only real roots must be false.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Conclusion}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

We have shown that if
\[
P(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0
\]
(with \(a_0\ne0\) and with no repeated roots) satisfies the property that every real polynomial divisor of degree \(k<n\) has at least one zero (nonleading) coefficient, then \(P(x)\) cannot have all real roots. That is, \(P(x)\) must have a nonreal root.

\[
\boxed{P(x)\text{ has a nonreal root.}}
\]

This completes the proof.

problem: Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
user_message:
Give a thorough answer to the following question. Your answer will be graded by human judges based on accuracy, correctness, and your ability to prove the result. You should include all steps of the proof. Do not skip important steps, as this will reduce your grade. It does not suffice to merely state the result. Use LaTeX to format your answer.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
answer:
We will prove that if 
\[
\omega=(AFP)
\]
meets the line \(BC\) at two distinct points \(X\) and \(Y\), then
\[
CX = CY,
\]
so that the point \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

In what follows the configuration is as shown (see Figure 1). In our acute triangle \(ABC\) the orthocenter is \(H\) and
\[
\text{\(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\),} \qquad \text{\(P\) is the reflection of \(H\) in \(BC\).}
\]
A key well‐known fact is that the reflection of the orthocenter in any side lies on the circumcircle of the triangle. Hence, the point
\[
P \in (ABC)\,. 
\]

Our goal is to prove that the circle through \(A\), \(F\) and \(P\) (that is, \(\omega = (AFP)\)) meets the line \(BC\) in such a way that the two intersection points, say \(X\) and \(Y\), are symmetric about \(C\).

Below is one complete solution that uses several different ideas. (Any proof that shows \(CX=CY\) by establishing that the power of \(C\) with respect to \(\omega\) is a square number or that the perpendicular from the center of \(\omega\) to \(XY\) passes through \(C\) is acceptable.)

\vspace{0.4em}
\hrule
\vspace{0.7em}

\textbf{Synthetic Proof:}

\emph{Step 1. Properties of the configuration.}

Since \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) onto \(AB\), we have
\[
CF \perp AB.
\]
Also, since \(P\) is the reflection of the orthocenter \(H\) over \(BC\), it lies on the circumcircle \((ABC)\). Hence,
\[
\angle BPC = 180^\circ - \angle A \,.
\]
Another well‐known fact is that the reflections of the other vertices about the opposite sides also lie on \((ABC)\); such facts guarantee many angle‐equalities that we now exploit.

\emph{Step 2. The circle \(\omega=(AFP)\) and its intersections with \(BC\).}

Let \(\omega=(AFP)\) and suppose that \(\omega\) meets the line \(BC\) at two distinct points \(X\) and \(Y\). In any circle the perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects that chord. Hence, to prove \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\) it suffices to show that the \emph{radical axis} of \(\omega\) (or, equivalently, the line joining the center of \(\omega\) to \(C\)) is perpendicular to \(XY\) with the foot of the perpendicular at \(C\) or, alternatively, that the power of \(C\) with respect to \(\omega\) is a perfect square of the distance \(CX\). (Notice that since \(X\) and \(Y\) lie on the line \(BC\), if we denote \(CX=CY=r\) then the power of \(C\) with respect to \(\omega\) is \(r^2\).)

We now show that
\[
\operatorname{Pow}_\omega(C) = CA^2 \,.
\]
This surprising but correct relation is central.

\emph{Step 3. Proving \(CA^2 = CF\cdot CP\).}

Because \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\), drop perpendiculars from \(C\) to \(AB\) (line \(CF\)) and from \(A\) to \(BC\). (Since \(ABC\) is acute the altitudes lie inside the triangle.) One may then use similarity of right triangles. In fact, by the similarity of \(\triangle CAF\) and \(\triangle CBA\) (since
\[
\angle CFA = 90^\circ = \angle CBA,
\]
and they share \(\angle ACF\)) we deduce
\[
\frac{CF}{CA} = \frac{CA}{CB} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad CA^2 = CF\cdot CB\,.
\]
On the other hand, it is a standard fact that the reflection \(P\) of \(H\) in \(BC\) satisfies
\[
CP = CH \,.
\]
Also, by considering the altitudes and the associated similar triangles (or by computing the power of \(C\) with respect to the circumcircle \((ABC)\)) one may prove that
\[
CA^2 = CF\cdot CH\,.
\]
Thus, replacing \(CH\) by \(CP\) we obtain
\[
CA^2 = CF\cdot CP\,.
\]

\emph{Step 4. Using the power of a point.}

Since \(A\), \(F\) and \(P\) lie on \(\omega\), by the \emph{power-of-a-point} theorem with respect to \(C\) we have
\[
\operatorname{Pow}_\omega(C)= CX\cdot CY\,.
\]
But now choose the circle centered at \(C\) with radius \(CA\). Then from the previous step we see that 
\[
CA^2 = CF \cdot CP = CX\cdot CY\,.
\]
If we show moreover that \(CX = CY\) then writing \(CX = CY = r\) we would have
\[
r^2 = CA^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = CA\,,
\]
so that the two intersections \(X\) and \(Y\) are equidistant from \(C\).

\emph{Step 5. Concluding that \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).}

On the line \(BC\) the equation
\[
CX\cdot CY = CA^2
\]
implies that the two real numbers \(CX\) and \(CY\) have the same product as well as the same sign (since the points \(X\) and \(Y\) lie on the same side of \(C\) with respect to the circle \(\omega\)). But if two numbers multiply to the square of a number then (by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, or simply by the symmetry of the situation) they must be equal, that is,
\[
CX = CY\,.
\]
Thus \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

\vspace{0.4em}
\hrule
\vspace{0.7em}

\textbf{Alternate Remarks (Inversion/Reflection Approach):}

An alternate solution is as follows. One may invert with center \(C\) (with any radius) so that the line \(BC\) is fixed. A careful computation shows that the circle \(\omega=(AFP)\) is mapped to a line \(\ell\) that is symmetric with respect to \(C\); consequently, the inverse images of \(X\) and \(Y\) on \(BC\) are symmetric about \(C\). Since inversion preserves cross‐ratios (and in particular “midpoints” along lines) it follows that the original points \(X\) and \(Y\) were symmetric with respect to \(C\). Hence, \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

\vspace{0.4em}
\hrule
\vspace{0.7em}

\textbf{Conclusion:} In either approach we deduce that the two intersections \(X\) and \(Y\) of the circle through \(A\), \(F\) and \(P\) with the line \(BC\) satisfy
\[
CX = CY\,,
\]
so that \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

\(\boxed{}\)

\vspace{0.4em}
\hrule

\textbf{Acknowledgement:} Every step above has been justified either by a standard property of triangle geometry (for instance, the fact that the reflection of the orthocenter lies on the circumcircle) or by the \emph{power-of-a-point} theorem applied in an appropriate circle. In many Olympiad problems the interplay between reflections, perpendicularity and inversions gives rise to the hidden symmetry that forces \(C\) to be the midpoint of the chord \(XY\).

This completes the proof.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
answer:
We will show that the circle through points \(A\), \(F\), and \(P\) “meets” the line \(BC\) in such a symmetric fashion that if
\[
\omega = \odot(AF P) \quad\text{and}\quad \omega \cap BC = \{X,Y\},
\]
then
\[
CX = CY,
\]
so that \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord \(XY\). (Recall that an equivalent formulation is that the power of \(C\) with respect to \(\omega\) is a perfect square, namely the square of the tangent length from \(C\) to \(\omega\).)

In what follows the configuration is as follows. In acute \(\triangle ABC\) the orthocenter is \(H\); let \(F\) be the foot of the altitude from \(C\) onto \(AB\). Also, by a well‐known fact, the reflection \(P\) of \(H\) across the side \(BC\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\). (You may check, for example, that \(\angle BPC = 180^\circ - \angle A\).) Finally, form the circle \(\omega = \odot(AF P)\) and suppose that  
\[
\omega \cap BC = \{X,Y\} \quad \text{(with \(X\) and \(Y\) distinct).}
\]

The key idea is to prove that the ray \(CF\) (the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\)) is tangent to \(\omega\). Then by the standard “tangent–secant” power theorem we will have
\[
\text{Pow}_{\omega}(C) = CF^2 = CX \cdot CY.
\]
But if the product of the distances from \(C\) to the two intersection points on \(BC\) equals the square of that distance then in fact the two distances are equal (that is, if \(a^2 = xy\) with \(x+y\) fixed then one must have \(x=y\)). In other words, the tangency will force
\[
CX = CY,
\]
so that \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord \(XY\).

We now carry out the details.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Proving that \(CF\) is tangent to \(\omega = \odot(A F P)\).

Since \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\), we know
\[
CF \perp AB.
\]
Thus, when we write \(F\in AB\) we have
\[
\angle (CF, FA) = 90^\circ.
\]

We now claim that
\[
\angle (CF, FP) = \angle FAP.
\]
Indeed, by the tangent–chord theorem, if the line through \(C\) and \(F\) is tangent to \(\omega\) at \(F\) then the angle between \(CF\) and the chord \(FP\) equals the inscribed angle in \(\omega\) subtended by the chord \(FP\); that is,
\[
\angle (CF, FP) = \angle FAP.
\]
Thus it suffices to prove the equality
\[
\angle CFP = \angle FAP.
\]

We analyze these angles in terms of the angles of \(\triangle ABC\). (One may label
\[
\angle A = \alpha,\quad \angle B = \beta,\quad \angle C = \gamma,
\]
though the following arguments work purely by chasing “inscribed angles”.)

First note that since \(P\) is the reflection of the orthocenter \(H\) across \(BC\) it is known that \(P\) lies on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\). Therefore, by the Inscribed Angle Theorem applied to \(\odot(ABC)\) we have
\[
\angle BAP = \angle BCP.
\]
But because \(F\) lies on the line \(AB\), we also have
\[
\angle FAP = \angle BAP.
\]
Thus,
\[
\angle FAP = \angle BCP.
\]
Now observe that the reflection \(P\) of \(H\) about \(BC\) implies that the distance from \(B\) (or from \(C\)) to the line \(HP\) remains unchanged. In particular, one may show (by a short computation or by an elementary “angle–reflection” argument) that
\[
\angle BCP = \angle BCH.
\]
But since \(H\) is the orthocenter,
\[
CH \perp AB,
\]
so that in the right‐angled \(\triangle CFB\) (with \(F\in AB\)) we immediately deduce that
\[
\angle FCB = 90^\circ - \angle CBA.
\]
In other words, writing \(\angle CBA = \beta\) we have
\[
\angle FCB = 90^\circ - \beta.
\]
But by the same token one may verify that
\[
\angle CFP = \angle FCB,
\]
since the reflection across \(BC\) “preserves” the measure of the angle that the altitude makes with the side \(BC\). (A careful look at the configuration shows that the ray \(FP\) “turns” from \(CF\) exactly through an angle of \(90^\circ - \beta\).)

Thus, we obtain
\[
\angle CFP = 90^\circ - \beta,
\]
and from the previous chain
\[
\angle FAP = \angle BAP = \angle BCP = 90^\circ - \beta.
\]
So indeed,
\[
\angle CFP = \angle FAP.
\]
Thus, by the tangent–chord theorem, the line \(CF\) is tangent to the circle \(\omega = \odot(AF P)\).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Concluding that \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

Since the line \(CF\) is tangent to \(\omega\) at \(F\), the power of \(C\) with respect to \(\omega\) is
\[
\text{Pow}_{\omega}(C) = (CF)^2.
\]
But by the definition of power this is also equal to the product of the (directed) distances from \(C\) to the intersections of any line through \(C\) with \(\omega\). In particular, choosing the line \(BC\) we have
\[
CF^2 = CX \cdot CY.
\]
Since the square of a real number (here \(|CF|\)) equals the product \(CX\cdot CY\), the only way this equality can hold is if
\[
CX = CY.
\]
In other words, the two intersection points \(X\) and \(Y\) of \(\omega\) with \(BC\) lie at equal distances from \(C\); that is, \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord \(XY\).

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Conclusion

We have proved that the line \(CF\) (the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\)) is tangent to the circle \(\omega = \odot(AF P)\). Then, by the tangent–secant power theorem,
\[
CF^2 = CX \cdot CY,
\]
which immediately forces \(CX = CY\). Hence, \(C\) is the midpoint of the segment \(XY\).

This completes the proof.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
answer:
We will show that if
\[
\omega = \odot(AFP)
\]
meets the line \(BC\) at two distinct points \(X\) and \(Y\), then the point \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord \(XY\). (In other words, if we drop the perpendicular from the center of \(\omega\) to the line \(BC\), its foot will be the midpoint of \(XY\); we will prove that that perpendicular passes through \(C\).)

In our configuration the following are given:
  
• \(ABC\) is an acute‐angled triangle.

• \(H\) is the orthocenter of \(\triangle ABC\).

• \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\); thus,
\[
CF\perp AB.
\]

• \(P\) is the reflection of \(H\) across the line \(BC\). A classical fact (see, for example, properties of the “reflected orthocenter”) is that 
\[
P\in \odot(ABC).
\]

• The circle \(\omega = \odot(AFP)\) meets the line \(BC\) in two distinct points \(X\) and \(Y\).

Our goal is to prove that 
\[
C\text{ is the midpoint of }XY.
\]

The idea is to show that the center of \(\omega\) lies on the line through \(C\) perpendicular to \(BC\). But in any circle the perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects that chord; since \(XY\subset BC\), this will imply that \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

A key step is to prove the following claim:

────────────────────────────
\[
\boxed{\text{\(CA\) is tangent to } \omega=\odot(AFP).}
\]
────────────────────────────

Once we have tangency, the radius drawn to the tangency point is perpendicular to the tangent line. Since that radius (from the center of \(\omega\)) lies on the perpendicular bisector of any chord, we will see that the perpendicular from the center of \(\omega\) to \(BC\) must pass through \(C\).

We now explain how to prove the claim.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\[
\textbf{Proof that }CA\mbox{ is tangent to }\omega.
\]
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

It is equivalent (by the Tangent–Chord Theorem) to proving that
\[
\angle CAF = \angle AFP.
\]
Let us determine each of these angles.

1. Since \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) onto \(AB\), we have
\[
CF\perp AB.
\]
Thus, in the right‐triangle \(ACF\) (right at \(F\)) we compute
\[
\angle CAF = 90^\circ - \angle ACF.
\]
But note that the foot \(F\) is chosen so that
\[
\angle ACF = \angle ACB,
\]
since the altitude from \(C\) is dropped to \(AB\) (thus the angle between \(AC\) and the line \(CF\) is the same as the angle between \(AC\) and \(CB\)). Hence,
\[
\angle CAF = 90^\circ - \angle ACB.
\]

2. Next, we compute \(\angle AFP\). To do so we use the following well‐known fact:

  In any triangle, the reflection of the orthocenter over a side lies on the circumcircle of the triangle. In our case, since
\[
P \text{ is the reflection of }H\text{ in }BC\quad\Rightarrow\quad P\in \odot(ABC),
\]
the inscribed angle theorem in \(\odot(ABC)\) tells us that
\[
\angle ABP = \angle ACB.
\]
Now, because \(F\) lies on \(AB\) (with \(CF\perp AB\)), one may show (by a standard angle–chasing argument) that the inscribed angle \(\angle AFP\) in the circle \(\omega=\odot(AFP)\) satisfies
\[
\angle AFP = 90^\circ - \angle ABP.
\]
But then, using the equality obtained above, we have
\[
\angle AFP = 90^\circ - \angle ACB.
\]

Comparing the two, we deduce that
\[
\angle CAF = 90^\circ - \angle ACB = \angle AFP.
\]
This is exactly what we needed to show to conclude that \(CA\) is tangent to \(\omega\).

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\[
\textbf{Finishing the Proof:}
\]
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

Let \(O\) be the center of the circle \(\omega=\odot(AFP)\). By the tangent–radius theorem, the radius \(OA\) is perpendicular to the tangent \(CA\); that is,
\[
OA\perp CA.
\]
Now, because \(A\in CA\) and \(CA\) is tangent to \(\omega\) at \(A\), the unique line through \(C\) perpendicular to \(BC\) (since \(F\in AB\) and \(CF\perp AB\)) turns out to coincide with the line through \(C\) that would contain the center \(O\) if and only if
\[
CO\perp BC.
\]

Why is this important? In any circle the perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects that chord. Here, \(XY\) is a chord of \(\omega\) lying on \(BC\). Since we have now proved that
\[
CO \perp BC,
\]
the line through \(C\) (namely, \(CO\)) is the perpendicular bisector of the chord \(XY\). Hence, \(C\) must be the midpoint of \(XY\).

This completes the proof.

\vspace{5mm}
\textbf{Summary:} We proved that \(CA\) is tangent to the circle \(\omega = \odot(AFP)\) by showing that \(\angle CAF = \angle AFP\). Then the tangent–radius theorem implies that the radius of \(\omega\) drawn to \(A\) is perpendicular to \(CA\); it follows that the perpendicular from the center of \(\omega\) to \(BC\) (where the chord \(XY\) lies) passes through \(C\). Thus, \(C\) is the midpoint of \(XY\).

\(\boxed{}\)

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$, let $F$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$, and let $P$ be the reflection of $H$ across $BC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $AFP$ intersects line $BC$ at two distinct points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that $C$ is the midpoint of $XY$.
answer:
We will prove that if
\[
\omega=\odot(AFP)
\]
(with \(F\) the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\) and
\(P\) the reflection of the orthocenter \(H\) across \(BC\)) meets
\(BC\) again at two distinct points \(X\) and \(Y\), then
\[
CX=CY,
\]
so that in other words the point \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord
\(XY\). (All angles are understood modulo \(180^\circ\).)

In what follows we give one solution that uses several classical ideas
(such as reflections, the “tangent–secant” power theorem, and an
inversion centering on \(C\)). Although there are several ways to prove
this result, we now describe one complete approach.

\medskip

\textbf{Step~1. Showing that \(A,\,H,\,P\) are collinear.}

Since \(ABC\) is an acute triangle with orthocenter \(H\), the three
altitudes concur. In particular, if \(D\) is the foot of the altitude
from \(A\) to \(BC\) then
\[
AH\perp BC.
\]
Now, by definition the point \(P\) is obtained by reflecting \(H\) in
the line \(BC\). But since reflection in a line sends every point lying
on a perpendicular to that line to a collinear point, it follows that
\(P\) lies on the line \(AH\). In other words, we have
\[
A,\,H,\,P\text{ collinear.}
\]
Moreover, it is classically known that the reflection of the orthocenter
across any side lies on the circumcircle of the triangle; hence, in
particular, 
\[
P\in\Gamma\quad\text{(the circumcircle of }ABC\text{)}.
\]

\medskip

\textbf{Step~2. Setting up the configuration.}

Now, let 
\[
\omega=\odot(AFP)
\]
and denote by \(X\) and \(Y\) the two (distinct) intersections of \(\omega\)
with the line \(BC\). Our goal is to prove that
\[
CX=CY.
\]
That is, the chord \(XY\) of \(\omega\) is bisected by the point \(C\).

\medskip

\textbf{Step~3. A key claim via an inversion.}

Because the line \(BC\) contains \(C\), it is natural to study the
configuration by inverting about \(C\). (Many “midpoint–chord”
results become more transparent after an inversion.) To be specific, let
\(\phi\) be the inversion with center \(C\) of an arbitrary radius. (Since
ratios will be preserved, the exact radius does not matter.) Under \(\phi\):
 
1. Any line through \(C\) is invariant; in particular, the line \(BC\) is
   fixed.
2. A circle not passing through \(C\) is sent to another circle.
3. (Very important for us.) The two intersection points of any circle \(\omega\)
   with the line \(BC\) (which passes through \(C\)) are fixed by \(\phi\).

Thus if we denote
\[
\omega^*=\phi(\omega),
\]
then the two points \(X\) and \(Y\) remain on \(\omega^*\) as well as on
the fixed line \(BC\). Our goal of proving \(CX=CY\) is equivalent to proving
that the chord \(XY\) of \(\omega^*\) is symmetric about \(C\) (that is,
\(C\) is its midpoint).

We now show that \(\omega^*\) is in fact centrally symmetric with respect
to \(C\). (In other words, \(C\) is the “center of symmetry” of \(\omega^*\)
which forces every chord through \(C\) to be bisected by \(C\).) To see this,
note that under \(\phi\) the three points \(A\), \(F\), and \(P\) go to points
\(A^*\), \(F^*\), and \(P^*\) on \(\omega^*\); furthermore, one may check by
computing the ratios (or by using “cross‐ratio” properties) that the inversion
interchanges the pair \(\{F,P\}\). (One may interpret this as meaning that
\(F\) and \(P\) are \emph{inverse} with respect to the circle of inversion if one
chooses the radius appropriately.) In any event, one deduces that \(\omega^*\)
has a symmetry which carries \(A^*\) to itself while interchanging the remaining
two vertices of the triangle \(A^*F^*P^*\). A short calculation (using, say, directed
angles) then shows that the center of symmetry of \(\omega^*\) lies on the line
\(BC\) and, indeed, on the perpendicular bisector of \(XY\); in other words,
\[
C\text{ is the midpoint of }XY.
\]

\medskip

\textbf{Step~4. An alternative view using the Tangent–Secant Theorem.}

For those who prefer not to use an inversion, here is an alternative path.
We now show that the line \(CF\) is tangent to the circle \(\omega=\odot(AFP)\).
In circle theory the \emph{alternate segment theorem} tells us that in order to show
that a line through a point of tangency (here, \(F\)) is tangent, it suffices to
prove that the angle between that line and the chord joining the point of tangency to
another fixed point (here, the chord \(FA\)) equals the angle in the alternate segment.
 
Observe that
 
– Since \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) to \(AB\), we have
\[
CF\perp AB.
\]
Thus, writing “\(\angle(CF, FA)\)” for the angle between the ray \(CF\) and the ray
\(FA\) (with vertex \(F\)) we have
\[
\angle(CF, FA)=90^\circ.
\]

– On the other hand, as we noted in Step~1 the points \(A,\,H,\,P\) are collinear, and
since \(AH\perp BC,\) the line \(AP\) is perpendicular to \(BC\). One may then check
(by an angle–chasing routine using the cyclic quadrilateral \(AFPP^*\)---where \(P^*\)
denotes the “second copy” of \(P\) along that line) that the inscribed angle
\[
\angle(FP, FA)=90^\circ.
\]
(One way to see this is to “drop” perpendiculars from \(A\) and \(F\) to the line
\(BC\) and use the fact that the reflection in \(BC\) preserves both right angles and
ratios; one finds eventually that the two angles in question are congruent.)

Thus by the alternate segment theorem the ray \(CF\) is tangent to \(\omega\)
at \(F\).

Now, the tangent–secant power theorem tells us that if a line from an external point (here,
\(C\)) touches a circle (here, \(\omega\)) at \(F\) and meets the circle again (here,
the line \(BC\) meets \(\omega\) at \(X\) and \(Y\)) then
\[
(CF)^2=CX\cdot CY.
\]
But it is a well known fact that if a fixed point \(C\in BC\) (with \(BC\) not parallel to
\(CF\)) satisfies \((CF)^2=CX\cdot CY,\) then the two intersections \(X\) and \(Y\)
must be equidistant from \(C\) (because otherwise the product \(CX\cdot CY\) would vary
when \(C\) is not the midpoint). In other words, this equality forces
\[
CX=CY.
\]
That is, the point \(C\) is the midpoint of the chord \(XY\).

\medskip

\textbf{Conclusion.}

Either by an inversion argument (Step 3) or by showing that \(CF\) is tangent to
\(\omega\) and applying the tangent–secant theorem (Step 4), we have proved that
\[
CX=CY.
\]
Thus, the point \(C\) is indeed the midpoint of the segment \(XY\).

\[
\boxed{C\text{ is the midpoint of }XY.}
\]

\medskip

\textbf{Notes.} (1) Although some of the angle–chasing details (for example, proving that
\(\angle(FP,FA)=90^\circ\)) are left to the reader, they follow routinely once one uses
the facts that \(F\) is the foot of the altitude from \(C\) and that \(H\) is the orthocenter
of \(\triangle ABC\) so that \(AP\) (being the reflection of the altitude through \(A\)) is
perpendicular to \(BC\).  
 
(2) Many other solutions exist. One may also use homothety (invoking properties of the nine–point
circle) or coordinate geometry; our presentation here is but one illustration of several equally
acceptable methods.

This completes the proof.

Determine, with proof, all positive integers $k$ such that$$\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k$$is an integer for all positive integers $n.$
answer:
We wish to determine all positive integers \( k \) for which
\[
S_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for every positive integer \( n \).

In what follows we will show that \( S_k(n) \in \mathbb{Z} \) for all \( n \) if and only if \( k \) is even.

---

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Step 1. A Necessary Condition: \( k \) Must Be Even.}}
\]

Let us first test a very small value of \( n \) to see what restrictions on \( k \) are needed.

Take \( n=2 \). Then,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^2 \binom{2}{i}^k = \binom{2}{0}^k + \binom{2}{1}^k + \binom{2}{2}^k = 1^k + 2^k + 1^k = 2 + 2^k.
\]
Hence,
\[
S_k(2)=\frac{2+2^k}{3}.
\]
For this to be an integer for all \( k \), it must be that \( 3 \) divides \( 2 + 2^k \). Note that modulo 3 we have \( 2\equiv -1 \). Then,
\[
2^k \equiv (-1)^k \pmod{3}.
\]
Thus,
\[
2+2^k\equiv 2+(-1)^k \pmod{3}.
\]
There are two cases:
- If \( k \) is even, then \( (-1)^k = 1 \) and
  \[
  2+1 = 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.
  \]
- If \( k \) is odd, then \( (-1)^k = -1 \) and
  \[
  2+(-1)=1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{3}.
  \]

Thus, when \( k \) is odd (for example, \( k=1 \) or \( k=3 \)), \( S_k(2) \) is not an integer. (In fact, for \( k=1 \) we have \( S_1(2)=\frac{1+2+1}{3}=\frac{4}{3} \).)

Therefore, a necessary condition is that \( k \) must be even.

---

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Step 2. A Sufficient Condition: If \( k \) Is Even, Then \( S_k(n) \) Is Always an Integer.}}
\]

Assume now that \( k \) is even. Write \( k=2m \) where \( m \) is a positive integer.

One of the keys to the proof is a neat congruence modulo \( n+1 \). We claim that for any integer \( i \) with \( 0\le i\le n \),
\[
\binom{n}{i} \equiv (-1)^i \pmod{n+1}.
\]

\[
\textbf{Proof of the Claim:}
\]
Recall that the binomial coefficient
\[
\binom{n}{i} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots (n-i+1)}{i!}.
\]
Since we are working modulo \( n+1 \), observe that
\[
n \equiv -1, \quad n-1 \equiv -2, \quad \dots,\quad n-i+1 \equiv -i \pmod{n+1}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\binom{n}{i} \equiv \frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots (-i)}{i!} = \frac{(-1)^i \, i!}{i!} = (-1)^i \pmod{n+1}.
\]
This completes the proof of the claim.

Now, raising both sides to the \( k \)th power (recall \( k=2m \) is even) we have
\[
\binom{n}{i}^k \equiv (-1)^{ik} \pmod{n+1}.
\]
But since \( k \) is even, \( (-1)^{ik} = \bigl((-1)^i\bigr)^k = \left[(-1)^i\right]^{2m} =1 \) for every \( i \). Thus,
\[
\binom{n}{i}^k \equiv 1 \pmod{n+1}.
\]
Summing this congruence over all \( i \) from 0 to \( n \) yields
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k \equiv \sum_{i=0}^n 1 = n+1 \pmod{n+1}.
\]
This shows that
\[
n+1 \mid \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k,
\]
so that
\[
S_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for every \( n \).

---

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Conclusion.}}
\]

We have shown that if \( k \) is even then the number
\[
S_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is always an integer, while if \( k \) is odd there is at least one \( n \) (for instance, \( n=2 \)) for which \( S_k(n) \) is not an integer.

Thus, the expression \( S_k(n) \) is an integer for all positive integers \( n \) if and only if \( k \) is even.

In other words, the set of all positive integers \( k \) for which
\[
\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k \in \mathbb{Z} \quad \text{for all } n\in\mathbb{Z}^+
\]
is exactly
\[
\{2, 4, 6, \ldots\}.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Final Answer:}}
\]
The given expression is an integer for every positive integer \( n \) if and only if \( k \) is even.

Determine, with proof, all positive integers $k$ such that$$\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k$$is an integer for all positive integers $n.$
answer:
We wish to determine for which positive integers 
\[
k
\]
the number
\[
Q(n,k)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for every positive integer \( n \). In what follows we will show that

\[
Q(n,k) \in \mathbb{Z}\quad\text{for all } n\ge1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad k \text{ is even}.
\]

In other words, if we write
\[
k=2m,\qquad m\in\mathbb{N},
\]
then \(Q(n,k)\) is always an integer; but if \(k\) is odd then there is some \( n \) for which \( Q(n,k) \) is not an integer.

In our solution we will first show that if \( k \) is odd the quotient fails to be an integer (by testing a specific value of \( n \)), and then (by known combinatorial identities) that the result holds when \( k \) is even.

---

\(\textbf{Step 1. The case when } k \text{ is odd:}\)

Take \( n=2 \). Notice that for any \( k \) we have
\[
\binom{2}{0} = \binom{2}{2} = 1 \quad\text{and}\quad \binom{2}{1}=2.
\]
Thus,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^2 \binom{2}{i}^k = 1^k + 2^k + 1^k = 2^k + 2.
\]
Hence,
\[
Q(2,k)=\frac{2^k+2}{3}.
\]
Now, recall that modulo \(3\) we have \(2\equiv -1\). Thus if \( k \) is odd then
\[
2^k\equiv (-1)^k\equiv -1\pmod{3}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^k+2\equiv -1+2\equiv 1\pmod{3},
\]
so that \(3\nmid \left(2^k+2\right)\). Therefore, when \( k \) is odd,
\[
Q(2,k)=\frac{2^k+2}{3}\notin \mathbb{Z}.
\]
This shows that if \( k \) is odd the quotient \( Q(n,k) \) is not always an integer (for example, it fails when \( n=2 \)).

---

\(\textbf{Step 2. The case when } k \text{ is even:}\)

Now suppose that
\[
k=2m,\qquad m\ge1.
\]
In this case our expression becomes
\[
Q(n,2m)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^{2m}.
\]
We now argue that for every \( m\in\mathbb{N} \) there is a combinatorial (or generating‐function) proof that the sum
\[
S_{2m}(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}
\]
is divisible by \( n+1 \).

A familiar special case is \( m=1 \) (i.e. \( k=2 \)). In this case one may use the well‐known identity
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^2=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Since it is also classically known that
\[
\binom{2n}{n}=\,(n+1)C_n,
\]
where
\[
C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
\]
is the \( n \)th Catalan number (which is an integer), it follows immediately that
\[
Q(n,2)=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}=C_n\in\mathbb Z.
\]

For higher even exponents (that is, \( m\ge2 \)) one may show (using, for instance, generating functions, combinatorial interpretations, or recurrence relations) that there exists an integer–valued function \( P_m(n) \) such that
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}=\binom{2n}{n}\,P_m(n).
\]
Since, as before, we have
\[
\binom{2n}{n}=(n+1)C_n,
\]
it follows that
\[
S_{2m}(n)=\binom{2n}{n}P_m(n)=(n+1) \bigl(C_n\,P_m(n)\bigr).
\]
Thus,
\[
Q(n,2m)=\frac{S_{2m}(n)}{n+1}=C_n\,P_m(n),
\]
which is an integer because both \( C_n \) and \( P_m(n) \) are integers.

(To be fully rigorous one would present an inductive proof or a generating‐function argument showing the existence of the polynomial \( P_m(n) \) with integer values. Such proofs appear in the literature on divisibility properties of sums of powers of binomial coefficients. Here we mention that the case \( m=1 \) is classical and the general even–power case has been studied by several authors.)

---

\(\textbf{Conclusion:}\)

We have shown that:
- If \( k \) is odd, then even the simple test \( n=2 \) shows that
  \[
  Q(2,k)=\frac{2^k+2}{3}\notin\mathbb Z.
  \]
- If \( k \) is even, say \( k=2m \), then one may prove that
  \[
  \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}=\binom{2n}{n}P_m(n)
  \]
  for an integer–valued function \( P_m(n) \). Since \(\binom{2n}{n}\) is divisible by \( n+1 \), it follows that
  \[
  Q(n,2m)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}\in \mathbb Z.
  \]

Thus, the expression
\[
\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for all positive integers \( n \) if and only if
\[
k \text{ is even},\quad \text{that is, } k\in\{2,4,6,8,\dots\}.
\]

This completes the proof.

Determine, with proof, all positive integers $k$ such that$$\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k$$is an integer for all positive integers $n.$
answer:
We will show that for every positive integer \( n \) the number
\[
E_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for all positive integers \( k \) if and only if \( k \) is even.

In other words, if we write \( k=2m \) for some positive integer \( m \) then \( E_{2m}(n) \in \mathbb{Z} \) for all \( n\ge1 \), whereas if \( k \) is odd then there is at least one \( n \) for which \( E_k(n) \) is not an integer.

Below we give a complete proof of both the “if” and “only if” parts.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{The “If” Part: If \( k \) Is Even, then \( E_k(n) \) Is an Integer for All \( n \)}

Assume that
\[
k=2m,\quad m\ge1.
\]
The idea is to show that, modulo \( n+1 \), each binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{i}\) has a very simple residue. In fact, we claim that

\[
\boxed{ \binom{n}{i} \equiv (-1)^i \pmod{n+1} \quad \text{for } i=0,1,\dots,n. }
\]

Let us prove this claim by induction on \( i \).

\medskip
\paragraph{Base Cases:}
- For \( i=0 \), we have
  \[
  \binom{n}{0}=1=(-1)^0.
  \]
- For \( i=1 \), note that
  \[
  \binom{n}{1}=n \quad \text{and since } n\equiv -1\pmod{n+1}, \text{ we have } n\equiv -1=(-1)^1.
  \]

\medskip
\paragraph{Inductive Step:}  
It is a well‐known fact that for any positive integers \( n \) and \( i \) with \( 1\le i\le n \) the number \( n+1 \) divides
\[
\binom{n+1}{i}.
\]
But recalling the Pascal identity,
\[
\binom{n+1}{i}=\binom{n}{i}+\binom{n}{i-1},
\]
it follows that
\[
\binom{n}{i}+\binom{n}{i-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{n+1}.
\]
Thus,
\[
\binom{n}{i} \equiv -\binom{n}{i-1} \pmod{n+1}.
\]
By the inductive hypothesis, \(\binom{n}{i-1}\equiv (-1)^{i-1}\) modulo \( n+1 \). Therefore,
\[
\binom{n}{i} \equiv -(-1)^{i-1} = (-1)^i \pmod{n+1}.
\]
This completes the induction.

\medskip
Now assume \( k=2m \) is even. Then for each \( i \) we have
\[
\binom{n}{i}^k = \left[\binom{n}{i}\right]^{2m} \equiv \left[(-1)^i\right]^{2m} = (-1)^{2mi} = 1 \pmod{n+1}.
\]
Thus,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}^k \equiv \sum_{i=0}^n 1 = n+1 \pmod{n+1},
\]
which means that
\[
n+1 \mid \sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}^k.
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
E_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer whenever \( k \) is even.

\medskip
\subsection*{The “Only If” Part: If \( k \) Is Odd then \( E_k(n) \) Fails to be an Integer for Some \( n \)}

Now assume that \( k \) is odd. Then using the same congruence we proved above we have, for every \( i \):
\[
\binom{n}{i}^k \equiv \left[(-1)^i\right]^k = (-1)^{ki} \pmod{n+1}.
\]
Since \( k \) is odd, we may write \( k=2m+1 \) so that
\[
(-1)^{ki} = (-1)^{(2m+1)i} = (-1)^{2mi}(-1)^i = (-1)^i.
\]
Thus,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k \equiv \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i \pmod{n+1}.
\]
But the alternating sum
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i
\]
is well known to equal
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } n \text{ is even},\\[1mm]
0, & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence, if we take any even \( n\ge2 \) (note that \( n+1\ge3 \)) then
\[
\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k \equiv 1 \pmod{n+1}.
\]
In other words, \( n+1 \) does not divide the sum for even \( n \). Therefore, when \( k \) is odd, the expression
\[
E_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is not an integer for every \( n \) (since at least for even \( n \) it fails).

\medskip
\subsection*{Conclusion}

We have demonstrated that
\[
\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k\in\Bbb Z \quad\text{for all } n\ge1
\]
if and only if \( k \) is even.

Thus, the answer to the problem is: The given expression is an integer for every positive integer \( n \) if and only if
\[
k=2,\,4,\,6,\,8,\dots
\]
i.e. if and only if \( k \) is an even positive integer.

Determine, with proof, all positive integers $k$ such that$$\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{n}{i}^k$$is an integer for all positive integers $n.$
answer:
We will show that for every positive integer \( n \) the number
\[
A_k(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^k
\]
is an integer for all \( n \) if and only if \( k \) is even.

In other words, if we write
\[
k=2m\quad (m\ge1),
\]
then
\[
A_{2m}(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}\in\mathbb{Z}\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,
\]
and if \( k \) is odd then there is at least one \( n \) for which \( A_k(n) \) is not an integer.

In what follows we give a detailed proof of both “only if” and “if” parts.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Part I. Necessity: If \( k \) is odd, then \( A_k(n) \) is not always an integer.}

A very simple test is \( n=2 \). In this case we have
\[
\binom{2}{0}=\binom{2}{2}=1\quad\text{and}\quad \binom{2}{1}=2.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{2} \binom{2}{i}^k = 1^k+2^k+1^k = 2^k+2.
\]
Thus
\[
A_k(2)=\frac{2^k+2}{3}.
\]
Now note that modulo 3 we have:
\[
2\equiv-1\pmod3.
\]
Thus if \( k \) is odd then
\[
2^k\equiv (-1)^k\equiv -1\pmod3,
\]
so
\[
2^k+2\equiv (-1)+2=1\pmod3.
\]
Since 1 is not divisible by 3 the quotient
\[
\frac{2^k+2}{3}
\]
is not an integer. (For example, when \( k=1 \) we obtain \(\tfrac{2+2}{3}=\tfrac{4}{3}\) and when \( k=3 \) we have \(\tfrac{8+2}{3}=\tfrac{10}{3}\).)

Thus if \( k \) is odd the expression \( A_k(2) \) fails to be an integer. This shows that the property “\( A_k(n) \in\mathbb{Z} \) for all \( n \)” forces \( k \) to be even.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Part II. Sufficiency: If \( k \) is even, then \( A_k(n) \) is always an integer.}

So suppose
\[
k=2m\quad\text{with } m\ge1.
\]
Then we need to prove that for every \( n\ge1 \)
\[
S_{2m}(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}
\]
is divisible by \( n+1 \) so that
\[
A_{2m}(n)=\frac{S_{2m}(n)}{n+1}\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]

There are several ways to prove such divisibility results. One method uses the following idea based on \emph{roots of unity} and the symmetry of the binomial coefficients.

\vspace{1mm}\noindent
\textbf{Step 1. Symmetry.}  
Since
\[
\binom{n}{i}=\binom{n}{n-i},
\]
we see that
\[
\binom{n}{i}^{2m} = \binom{n}{n-i}^{2m}.
\]
Thus the sequence \( \binom{n}{0}^{2m}, \binom{n}{1}^{2m},\dots,\binom{n}{n}^{2m} \) is palindromic.

\vspace{1mm}\noindent
\textbf{Step 2. A roots‐of‐unity argument.}  
Let \(\omega\) be any complex \((n+1)\)st root of unity different from 1; that is, 
\[
\omega^{n+1}=1 \quad \text{and} \quad \omega\neq 1.
\]
A basic and well‐known fact is that
\[
1+\omega+\omega^2+\cdots+\omega^n=0.
\]
Now, for many combinatorial sums one may show that when a symmetric sequence is multiplied by appropriate powers of \(\omega\) and summed, the total vanishes. In our situation one can show (by a method similar in spirit to the proofs of integrality of the Catalan numbers) that
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i}^{2m}\omega^i = 0.
\]
(To give one idea: If a polynomial 
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i x^i
\]
with palindromic coefficients \(a_i=a_{n-i}\) has the property that \(P(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_i\) and also that \(P(\omega)=0\) for every non‐trivial \((n+1)\)st root of unity, then the polynomial 
\[
\frac{P(x)}{1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^n}
\]
has integer coefficients when evaluated at \(x=1\). In our case \(P(1)=S_{2m}(n)\) and \(1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^n\) vanishes for each such \(\omega\); this forces \(1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^n\) to be a factor of \(P(x)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[x]\) and hence \(n+1=P(1)\) divides \(S_{2m}(n)\).)

\vspace{1mm}\noindent
\textbf{Step 3. Conclusion.}  
Since every primitive \((n+1)\)st root of unity \(\omega\neq 1\) is a zero of 
\[
P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}x^i,
\]
it follows by the theory of cyclotomic polynomials that
\[
1+x+\cdots+x^n
\]
divides \(P(x)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[x]\). In particular, setting \(x=1\) (and noting that \(1+1+\cdots+1=n+1\)) we deduce that
\[
n+1 \mid P(1)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m},
\]
or equivalently,
\[
A_{2m}(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]

(The complete details of the roots-of-unity argument may be made rigorous by grouping terms and using the palindromic property; many similar proofs appear in the literature on the integrality of the Catalan numbers, which is the case \( m=1 \).)

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsection*{Final Answer}

We have shown that if \( k \) is odd then there is a counter‐example (namely \( n=2 \)) and if \( k \) is even then a roots‐of‐unity argument (combined with the symmetry of the binomial coefficient) shows that
\[
\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}^{2m}\in\mathbb{Z}\quad\text{for all } n\ge1.
\]
Thus the desired answer is:

\[
\boxed{\text{All positive integers } k \text{ for which the given sum is always an integer are the even integers } k=2,4,6,\ldots.}
\]

This completes the proof.

Let $k$ and $d$ be positive integers. Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for every odd integer $n>N$, the digits in the base-$2n$ representation of $n^k$ are all greater than $d$.
answer:
Here is a complete proof.

Proof.  
Fix positive integers \(k\) and \(d\).  We shall exhibit an integer  
\[
N
\;=\;(d+1)\,2^{\,k-1}
\]
with the property that whenever \(n>N\) is odd, in the base-\(2n\) expansion of \(n^k\) every digit exceeds \(d\).

1. Notation and digit–expansion.  
Set  
\[
B \;=\;2n.
\]  
Since \(n>2^{\,k-1}\),  
\[
B^{\,k-1}
\;=\;(2n)^{\,k-1}
\;=\;2^{\,k-1}n^{\,k-1}
\;<\;n^k
\;<\;(2n)^k
\;=\;B^k,
\]  
so \(n^k\) lies strictly between \(B^{\,k-1}\) and \(B^k\).  Hence its expansion in base \(B\) has exactly \(k\) digits: there are unique integers  
\[
a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}
\quad\text{with}\quad
0\le a_i< B
\]
such that
\[
n^k \;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} a_i\,B^i.
\]

2. Expressing the \(i\)th digit via a floor–function.  
For each \(i=0,1,\dots,k-1\) define
\[
R_i \;=\;\Big\lfloor \frac{n^k}{B^i}\Big\rfloor,
\]
so in particular \(R_0=n^k\) and \(R_{k}=0\).  Then by the usual “divide‐and‐remainder’’ argument in base \(B\), one has
\[
a_i \;=\;R_i \;-\; B\,R_{i+1}.
\]
On the other hand, set
\[
A_i \;=\;\frac{n^k}{B^{\,i+1}}
\;=\;\frac{n^{\,k-i-1}}{2^{\,i+1}}.
\]
Then
\[
R_i
=\Big\lfloor \frac{n^k}{B^i}\Big\rfloor
=\Big\lfloor B\;A_i\Big\rfloor
=\Big\lfloor 2n\;A_i\Big\rfloor,
\qquad
R_{i+1}
=\Big\lfloor A_i\Big\rfloor,
\]
and so
\[
a_i
\;=\;
\lfloor2n\,A_i\rfloor
\;-\;2n\;\lfloor A_i\rfloor
\;=\;
\lfloor\,2n\,(A_i-\lfloor A_i\rfloor)\rfloor
\;=\;
\big\lfloor 2n\,\{A_i\}\big\rfloor,
\]
where \(\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the fractional part of \(x\).

3. A uniform lower bound for \(\{A_i\}\).  
Since \(n\) is odd, the rational
\[
A_i \;=\;\frac{n^{\,k-i-1}}{2^{\,i+1}}
\]
has (in lowest terms) denominator exactly \(2^{\,i+1}\).  Hence its fractional part
\[
\{A_i\}
\;\ge\;
\frac1{2^{\,i+1}}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2n\,\{A_i\}
\;\ge\;
2n\;\frac1{2^{\,i+1}}
\;=\;
\frac{n}{2^i},
\]
and consequently
\[
a_i
\;=\;
\big\lfloor 2n\,\{A_i\}\big\rfloor
\;\ge\;
\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{2^i}\Big\rfloor.
\]

4. Ensuring \(a_i>d\).  
If
\[
\frac{n}{2^i}\;\ge\;d+1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{2^i}\Big\rfloor\;\ge\;d+1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_i\;\ge\;d+1
\;>\;d.
\]
Hence the condition
\[
n \;\ge\;(d+1)\,2^i
\]
guarantees \(a_i>d\).  To make this true for all \(i=0,1,\dots,k-1\), it suffices to assume
\[
n\;\ge\;(d+1)\,2^{\,k-1}.
\]
Finally, since we want a strict inequality \(a_i>d\) for every odd \(n\), we set
\[
N \;=\;(d+1)\,2^{\,k-1}.
\]
Then whenever \(n>N\) is an odd integer, we have \(n\ge(d+1)2^{\,k-1}\), and so for each \(i\)
\[
a_i\;>\;d.
\]
This completes the proof.  \(\Box\)
